This game is fantastic. It's a better version of Yakuza 4. This time we play five characters (Kiryu, Saejima, Haruka, Akiyama and Shinada; Tanimura is no longer playable). 

I think the story is really great. In my opinion, it has the same level of hype and emotion as Yakuza 0. 

The graphics and soundtracks are also fantastic. 
It's also cool that we can play in five different locations in this game, whereas in the previous games there are only one or two locations available to explore.

But my highlight is the gameplay. The combat system is almost the same as Yakuza 0 and I got along well (much better than Yakuza 3 and 4). You can also automatically assign the points you earn when you level up. 
But that's not all. I think it's cool that the characters have different jobs: Kiryu as a cab driver (almost had a GTA vesion to Yakuza/Like a Dragon T_T), Saejima (then as the game progresses) as a hunter, Haruka as an idol pop star, Akiyama as a laid back loanshark (like in Yakuza 4), and Shinada as a journalist who used to be a baseball player. 

[spoiler]The game ends with a cliffhanger, and the story continues with Yakuza 6. Boy, am I glad I only discovered the game series last year. I'd be impatient if I had to wait a few years to see the game's sequel.[/spoiler]

Yakuza 5 Remastered stands as a monumental entry in the Yakuza series, offering an expansive and emotionally resonant experience that encapsulates the essence of the franchise. Released on Steam in January 2021, this remastered version enhances the original PlayStation 3 title with improved graphics and smoother performance, while preserving the intricate storytelling and diverse gameplay elements that fans cherish.

The game's narrative unfolds across five distinct chapters, each focusing on a different protagonist: Kazuma Kiryu, Taiga Saejima, Haruka Sawamura, Shinada Tatsuo, and returning character Shun Akiyama. This structure allows for a multifaceted exploration of themes such as ambition, redemption, and the pursuit of dreams. The interconnected stories culminate in a climactic finale that brings all characters together, delivering a satisfying and emotional conclusion to their individual arcs.

One of the standout features of Yakuza 5 Remastered is its vast array of minigames and side activities. From the exhilarating taxi driving missions in Fukuoka to the intense hunting expeditions in the snowy mountains of Hokkaido, the game offers a plethora of diversions that enrich the main storyline. The inclusion of "Another Drama" side stories provides additional depth to each character, allowing players to engage in unique activities tailored to their personalities and backgrounds.

The combat system has been refined, introducing new Heat Actions and special battle techniques for each protagonist. Kiryu's enhanced moveset, Saejima's powerful grappling techniques, and Shinada's unorthodox fighting style contribute to a dynamic and engaging combat experience. Haruka's rhythm-based dance battles offer a refreshing change of pace, showcasing the game's versatility in gameplay design.

Graphically, the remastered version showcases significant improvements over its predecessor. The environments are more detailed, character models are sharper, and animations are smoother, resulting in a visually appealing experience. While some minor glitches and texture issues persist, they do not detract from the overall quality of the game.

The soundtrack deserves special mention, featuring a diverse range of tracks that complement the game's tone and setting. From the upbeat tunes accompanying Haruka's idol performances to the intense battle themes, the music enhances the immersive experience and adds emotional weight to key moments.

However, Yakuza 5 Remastered is not without its flaws. The pacing can be uneven at times, with certain segments feeling drawn out or repetitive. Additionally, the game's vast content can be overwhelming, leading to moments where the sheer volume of activities may detract from the main narrative focus.

In conclusion, Yakuza 5 Remastered is a testament to the series' commitment to delivering rich, multifaceted storytelling and diverse gameplay experiences. Its expansive world, memorable characters, and engaging combat mechanics make it a must-play for fans of the franchise and newcomers alike. Despite its minor shortcomings, the game remains a standout entry in the Yakuza series, offering a comprehensive and satisfying adventure that will resonate with players long after the credits roll.

I've been playing through the Yakuza games, in order, because Kiryu's story is one of the best story archs given how much we see him grow and change. Yakuza 5 offers my favorite story beats (so far), especially for Kiryu and Haruka. Essentially, between 0-4 we've been with Kiryu for 22 years. I think in order to understand why Yakuza 5 is so impact, it's helpful to know Kiryu's and Haruka's journey to this point. 

Below is a summary of the events important to me leading up to Yakuza 5, specific to Kiryu and Haruka. 

[spoiler] Yakuza 0 (Kiryu: 20) sees Kiryu rise as the Dragon of Dojima. Yakuza 1 (Kiryu: 37, Haruka: 9) sees Kiryu lose both his best friend and the love of his life, while essentially adopting Haruka who has lost her mom; Kiryu gives us the Yakuza lifestyle so he can raise Haruka. Yakuza 2 (Kiryu: 38, Haruka: 10) sees Kiryu sucked back into the Yakuza to help establish a new leader for the Tojo Clan; Kiryu shares that his dream is to run an orphanage; Haruka is offered an idol position but turns it down. Yakuza 3 (Kiryu: 41, Haruka: 13) shows Kiryu running an orphanage with the help of Haruka; Kiryu defends his orphanage against the Yakuza. Yakuza 4 (Kiryu: 42, Haruka: 14) shows Haruka stepping up further and running the orphanage while Kiryu is once again forced to save the Tojo Clan. [/spoiler]

First and foremost, the random encounters are absolutely egregious! No other entry in the series compares to what this game did to random encounters. YOU WILL COME TO FEAR WALKING THE STREETS OF JAPAN! There were a couple of moments where I finished a random encounter only to enter a new one without moving a step and I swear there is no random encounters (outside of Victory Road) that have less than 5 dudes. It wore down my very soul. Every encounter had me fantasizing about Saw traps I'd place these hoodlums in while I mindlessly button mashed my way through the fights. Outside of all that, the game is pretty good. One of the best.

Plot has some of the issues that Yakuza 4 had with it feeling a bit too bloated, so when the different storylines begin to tie in with one another it gets a bit messy. As the plot moves along, there are what feels like 5 twists/reveals per hour so any sense of excitement or surprise that Yokoyama expected these moments to have on the audience is lost. The overarching antagonist's master plan is perhaps one of the most convoluted in the series, but if you choose not to get too caught up in all the details of his scheme he makes for an interesting and enjoyable villain.

I think I'm able to forgive these flaws because of just how grand and ambitious it all feels especially during Kiryu's strong opening plotline and the emotional finale. Some of the absolute highest points in the series are present here so even when it begins to lose my interest it draws me back in with great force. The sheer spectacle and scope make it hard not to get swept away in it all. I think it manages to stick the landing regardless of my criticisms.

Like in Y4, this entry has unique combat styles for each playable character. This is a nice step-up from the last game and I found Saejima to be the biggest improvement. In Y4, you need to invest quite a bit of time in Saejima's upgrades for the guy to be enjoyable to play, but here he is the best playing protagonist from the get go. Shinada is perhaps my least favorite combat-wise as result of his reliance on weapons. I never found weapons all that fun too use in this franchise outside of Ishin. Haruka gets dance-offs for her segment of the game and I was just so thankful to have a section of the game where I can enjoy the city without fear of 50 Japanese ruffians harassing me on my way to a takoyaki stand. Akiyama and Kiryu play about the same as in Y4 with few welcome changes.

There is an insane level of side content here primarily consisting of the side stories. Each character (except Akiyama) has their own side story which is basically an independent story arc and an accompanying minigame (these are notably more mechanically complex than previous Yakuza minigames).

Kiryu's is a combination of a taxi driving minigame where you carefully follow road laws and a 1v1 racing minigame. This one is my 2nd favorite only because the rubberbanding in the racing minigame was not balanced well. It was best to not use my heat at any point in the race except the absolute final stretch, otherwise the opponent will zoom past you if you have to large of a lead.

Saejima has a hunting minigame that starts off strong but eventually devolves into becoming a bit slow and tedious. Although, it did have one of the more interesting story arcs and every encounter with Yama-oroshi was exciting.

Haruka had my favorite side story as it contains several different minigames ranging from fan meet n greets, reporter interviews, game shows, and a lovely dancing rhythm game. The variety of content kept it feeling fresh all the way through the story arc.

I don't have much to say about Shinada's side story minigame other than that it was fine. It's actually pretty easy once you get heat eye from Igarashi's training (Igarashi's training as a whole is a pain in the ass tbh). I think it's necessary to do this one as the story arc offers some interesting insight into Shinada's character.

There was a handful of fun/quirky substories and some cute/heartwarming substories, but I didn't care for much of the ones I did in this entry. Honestly, that's fine by me because I had more than enough content to keep me busy with the side stories.

This isn't a major critique, but throughout these remastered Yakuza games I had this recurring issue where if I scrolled using my laptop's trackpad while my gamepad was connected it would cause some of the in-game menus to have an infinite scrolling bug that would only stop when I restarted the game. Also I did have trouble getting a couple achievements to pop in offline mode and had to reload saves on a few occasions to get them to pop.

Before I end this long word vomit, I want to say that I hope they bring back Shinada (maybe even Y4's Tanimura) in future games somehow. I understand that they don't have much of a place in mainline story due to their lack of a strong connection to the yakuza or other key characters in the franchise, but they might fit well in some small role within the Judgement series. I'd just like to see Shinada and Takasugi again. Such a fascinating relationship that surprisingly led to one of my favorite moments of the finale.

This is the beginning of the better Yakuza Games in terms of game quality if you're counting by release date.

Karaoke, every minigame, things you'd expect from around this time (Yakuza 0's release date) is here, if not just still a little bit janky.

Gameplay wise, its still as frustrating as Yakuza 4's combat, but less so just a tiny bit. Enemies block less but have unavoidable damaging moves you can do nothing but try and dodge against a invisible wall to get around. 

This game is one of the longer games out of the entire series next to 6 (third longest) and 0 (longest).

I think the missions with Taiga were annoying, especially up in the mountains and into the snowy city, I just powered through that entire section without doing any side content because of how annoying that whole city was with combat, you had to stick strictly to the sidewalks, no way to avoid enemies in your path other than just fighting, most of them had weapons that always stunned you.

Same with the 4th character that was playable, (not Haruka), his city was also annoying and his side content involved him getting better at baseball I guess. Didn't really know why he was even included besides having a Daigo subplot and boss fight.

Haruka's section was probably the best because its the first time we're allowed to control her or do anything with a female protagonist in the entire series. It did only consist of things like Dance battles and idol things, but I still believe that side of the game was probably more of a highlight than Akiyama's own story.

Weirdly Kiryu's side (while having the best combat) was lackluster, and consisted of a power scaling fight structure, where the devs would put him in a scenario where he would have to fight an escalating number of enemies each new game release. This time made it extremely ridiculous and hilarious, but also removes a lot of the tension because there's not much to lose for him until Yakuza 6 at this point.

Overall I think this game is one of the beginning of the good Yakuza games, in terms of release date. Everything after and up to Yakuza: Like a Dragon is some of the best content gaming has seen in years.

Yakuza 5 - The most ambitious game that RGG studio had ever done.

Story
- 5 Arcs. Each arc for each characters, except Haruka shared her arc with Akiyama, and the Final arc.
- You'll start with Kiryu then Saejima, Haruka and Akiyama then Shinada.
- Kiryu arc is pretty much straightforward. He tried to put his past behind, living as a taxi driver in Fukuoka when suddenly problems came to him. Again.
- Saejima arc tells the story when he's back to prison a year after event of Yakuza 4. Then things happened and he's now in Sapporo (the northern land of Japan, close to Russia).
- Haruka arc tells the story about her path to become an Jpop idol and somehow cross path with Akiyama in Sotenbori.
- Shinada arc tells the story about his struggle as a penniless writer who try to put his past about that faithful day 15 years ago, living as a freeloader in Nagoya when he discovered the dark truth.

Gameplay
- Probably the best fighting mechanic of the PS3 era Yakuza.
- A bit grindy. I finished this game in Normal and it's pretty sweaty to fight against bosses.
- Vast selection of minigames and side quest. Kiryu's Taxi driver, Saejima [spoiler]'s hunting the legendary bear[/spoiler], Haruka's activities as a J-idol and some insight into the Japanese entertainment with various cameo from irl and Shinada's battle against his former teammates.
- I'm not sure if Akiyama has one apart from dancing battle (overlapped with Haruka).

Sounds pretty much a good combination between the story and gameplay so what's the catch?
- Well. It's pretty much can be sum up by one sentence, "R1+A" simulator.
- I don't have exact number but I think this game could even surpass GTA V in terms of word count in the script.
- I mean - point at my hrs count - that's what I got even with holding R1+A to skip the dialog and skip cutscenes. I already finished this game once in another platform so I didn't miss anything.
- I'm pretty sure that if I play the game without skipping the dialog or cutscenes, the hrs count when finished the game would be double.

So just dialog simulator is the problem?
- No. The gameplay also dragging and the story writing is pretty much... not as bad as Y4 but dragging.
- They tried to do the same formula by telling the story of each character, build the background then sums that up in Tokyo, Kamurocho.
- The problem is by the time I finished Shinada arc, I don't recall what happened in Kiryu arc, and barely Saejima's, and had to rely on YT for summary. That's how dragging and the amount of sidestories/gameplay in later arc are.

So.. dialog simulator and dragging story?
- Another thing is that this game is grindy.
- For example, if you're playing on Hard or Legend difficulty I think you probably have to grind for a Tiger drop for both Kiryu and Saejima in the underground colossium.
- I didn't do that and I spent nearly 20 mins to fight against the boss with Kiryu, which could be just 5 mins or 10mins tops if I have tiger drop.
- Saejima also need to grind for his 3rd heavy attack to play this game a lot easier.
- While Haruka doesn't need that much of grinding, it would be nearly impossible to continue her main story without doing the side stories/tasks.
- Shinada is pretty much tragic. If you don't have any interest in baseball or his past (like me), his fight in the final arc is pretty much a nightmare. I finished his fight with health bar flashing.

... Akiyama?
- The problem with Akiyama is simple. "Why did Akiyama have to be in this game?".
- His story is ridiculously short, like 2-3 chapters and it shared with Haruka.
- And the writing is so damn bad like they just offed one significant character just for him to be there.
- I mean it'll be soooo much better if they didn't off that one character. Nobody cares about the characters that sprout from his arc.
- He had to be there just to get that final ending scene. But I don't buy it. They put him there just to make sure he's not the one off character like Tanimura in Y4.

Overall.
It's a good game but it's one of those game that "you finished once and never want to play again".
It's not  because of how bad the combat was like Yakuza 3.
It's not because of how empty the NG+ was like Yakuza 4.
It's just ... nobody wants to play another 30-40 hrs of dialogue simulator, grinding festival and a mediocre story.

And that's so unfortunate. Because this game is probably the most ambitious game RGG has ever done since. 
They dare to put 5 cities from Fukuoka, Sapporo, Osaka, Nagoya and Tokyo in one game. 5 biggest city in Japan. 
And we probably won't get anything like this again. Ever.

Yakuza 5. Where do I even begin? Yakuza 4 was a massive title, with 4 playable characters and a massive story that interconnected them all. Yakuza 5 does it all again, but this time, with 5 characters, and 5 individual maps. This game is ambitious as all hell, and it really does make every single character's story feel just as important as the others. Saejima and Akiyama both get a lot of screen time here, and it's all great stuff. The game has a very interesting and sometimes nonsensical story that brings all of our playable protagonists together, and the ending is as satisfying as it could have been. 

Whether you're hunting with Saejima, singing and dancing with Haruka, driving a taxi with Kiryu, or playing baseball with Tatsuo, Yakuza 5 locks you into an engaging story that entertains all the way through. A lot of people will tell you to skip this one. Don't. Yakuza 5 is as true to the series as all the games are, and I think it's got plenty to show for it.

I've left silly reviews for the other Yakuza games, but honestly I think this one deserves a proper one. Yakuza 5 is a great game. You should buy it. I could honestly just leave the review there. but what's the fun in that? In Y5, there are a total of 5 different characters, which is impressive for any singleplayer story game. 

First, there's the legendary Dragon of Dojima, Kiryu Kazuma, who is of course the main protagonist in every entry before this. He plays great, using a mix of his moves from 3 and 4, along with some new ones. His part really gives you the feels, and helps set up the story really well. 

Then, you have the "Slayer of Eighteen", Taiga Saejima, once again, another returning character. He feels really flushed out here, like they acknowledged the issues with his moveset in 4, and fixed him up to play better. His involvement in the story is really interesting too, and I think 5 did a great job hyping him up to be an equal to Kiryu. 

After Saejima, you have Haruka Sawamura, the adopted daughter of Kiryu Kazuma, who's appeared in every entry from 1-4. Her gameplay is much different than the others, which makes sense taking her into account as a character. She only has 2 chapters where you use her alone, which I think helps make that whole part much more welcoming for returning players. 

As for the second half of part 3, you can play as the man, the myth, the legend. The lifeline of Kamurocho himself, SHUN AKIYAMA!!! (Yes, he is my favorite character). Akiyama controls great here, they even gave him mid-air combos in his combat. His inclusion into the plot also works fine, although for the sake of keeping this review as spoiler free as possible, I won't dive into it. You end up switching between him and Haruka a lot in this part, but I honestly never had an issue with that. 

Last of all, in part 4 of the story, you play as Tatsuo Shinada, a character who only appears in Y5 and none of the other entries. He's easily the most unique character here, using weapons and throws primarily in his combat. He's a funny guy who lost everything, and I think his plot, albeit relatively self contained from the rest of the story, is still really good, and you get a feel for the guy. 

I guess in conclusion of this whole review though, if you've finished all the other Yakuza games from 0-4, definitively check out Yakuza 5, as it's amazing, and probably my new favorite game of all time.

Yakuza 5 really lives up to its reputation as the biggest of the series, so I will give it a big review,. Overall, it is easily one of my favourites, as each of the protagonists gets their own individual moment in the spotlight and - having now spent a good few hundred hours in the series - I feel like the characters are what makes these games so special.

Part 1: Taichi Suzuki (who happens to look a lot like Kiryu)
This might be the strongest Kiryu story so far. They added a lot of depth to his character and found a way to keep him interesting even though it is his 5th appearance as a protagonist. Seeing him deal with the consequences of his life and struggle to accept it really makes him seem more human than before. Most of his story is pretty down to earth and his interactions with his co-workers in his taxi driving side story are fantastic. Taxi-driving itself is probably my favourite mini-game in the entire series thus far.

Part 2: Saejima
Big, bad Saejima stole my heart in Yakuza 4 and he is incredible again in this one. Unfortunately, it starts off in prison again, but they introduced some really great new characters through it which had a really wholesome pay-off. They allowed him to have a bit more fun this time too with being able to go to karaoke and clubs, so we got to see more of his teddy bear side and it was great. His side story is about a hunting village in the freezing mountains and it was perfect for the character; 100%ing it got a bit tedious, but I still really liked it. Please can we have more games with Saejima?

Part 3: Akiyama/Haruka
This part is where we get to play as Yakuza's first female protagonist in high school Haruka. I enjoy rhythm games, so the dancing and concerts were fun for me (even if there were way too many of them on the job board missions). An idol is not exactly the direction I would have liked Haruka's character to go, but they presented it really well. I had always found the Japanese idol industry really creepy, but they showed me a side of it I had never considered before. I won't be buying tickets to a concert any time soon, but I did gain a newfound respect for the performers and their work. Haruka is a proper goody goody saint here and she does have some amazing moments, but I would really like to see a more interesting female lead some day. Her manager, Park, was a great character, but she didn't have a lot of screen time.

Akiyama is... there. I feel like there is so much potential for his character - it is such a unique and creative idea. He kind of takes a backseat to Haruka and plays the cool uncle who kicks ass (because God forbid they make Haruka able to fight her own battles). Akiyama deserves his own story instead of just being a convenient plot device for other characters, but I doubt we will ever see it.

Part 4: Shinada
The reason I wanted to write this long ass essay. I really thought Saejima would be my favourite character again, but then along came Shinada. Unlike the other characters who are over the top shounen badasses, Shinada is an absolute loser. As cool as Kiryu and the gang are, they are not very relatable to average people, but a broke loser who loves to get his balls rubbed? Now that is someone we can empathise with. Of course, he still has his crazy moments and has muscles like a roided up wrestler, but there is so much to relate to in his goofy charm. The translation team really did an awesome job with making his side-stories absolutely hilarious and I feel like they nailed his character. Minor spoiler, but there is a short scene where Shinada and his favourite prostitute (Milky-chan) share a magical moment on the rooftops before being crushed by reality. It was such an incredibly moving moment for me, because it was so human compared to the usual stories. Really an incredible character and it's a real shame they sent him to the "forgotten character" bin. I will say that the amount of guys in his story who are hung up on high school baseball days is kind of stupid, but when being a baseball player is his only plot significance, what else were they supposed to do?

Finale:
The finale is your typical Yakuza fare. Out of nowhere plot twists, hordes of trash enemies getting mowed down and last minute redemptions. It's a very long finale - even by Yakuza standards - but it is one of the better ones as each character gets their own moment. Also, for once Date wasn't randomly in a helicopter. The final boss was great (fight-wise... story-wise it is what you would expect by now) and overall I think this game really deserved more mainstream attention.

Yakuza 5 Remastered Review

I've just finished what might be my favorite Yakuza game! Here are my thoughts:


What I Loved:

Visuals/World: The expansive world design is a significant highlight. The fresh new accessible areas are not only visually impressive but also offer a diverse range of environments to explore.

Soundtrack: This Yakuza game once again delivers excellent music and track choices. It felt more like an award-winning movie than ever before.

Characters: Introducing a new playable character with a compelling story, alongside continuing the narratives of characters from Yakuza 4, was a great way to tie up loose ends and revisit familiar faces.

Combat: After the issues I had with Yakuza 3 and 4, I'm happy to say that the combat is enjoyable again in this game. The previous problems have been refined and are now much more appealing to play with.


What I Didn't Love:

Length: While I enjoyed much of the game and did a fair bit of exploration, the story felt drawn out at times. Specifically, the middle of Chapter 2, to just after the middle of Chapter 3 felt slow-paced. It's great if you want more Yakuza, but I personally skipped some side content to speed up my playthrough, even taking breaks to avoid burnout before reaching the better parts.


Recommendation: As with my other reviews, this is the second-to-last mainline Yakuza game featuring Kiryu, so I highly recommend playing it if you've completed the previous games. It could also serve as a good entry point as a trial run, but playing it as your first Yakuza game would mean missing a lot of context and potentially being confused.

Final Thoughts: Despite a slow section, I still consider this one of my favorite Yakuza games, ranking up there with Yakuza 0. There's so much to do and see, even surpassing Yakuza 0 in terms of the number of areas and characters. I found it incredibly engaging, and the story is once again fantastic. You'd be missing out if you skipped this for any reason! Be warned!

As has been the case with nearly every Yakuza game, Yakuza 5 takes what the previous game did and improves on it in nearly every way. From having more variety in the side missions, refining the combat systems, or adding new cities, Yakuza 5 is a nice improvement to Yakuza 4. However, even though Yakuza 5 is a great game, it has two giant flaws: the story and how ambitious it is. When it comes to the story, Yakuza 5 is very inconsistent and often drags on. Moreover, with the many different plot points, you end up forgetting what the main premise is. Outside of the story, Yakuza 5 is just way too ambitious. While I appreciate the amount of content and new ideas that have made their way into Yakuza 5, it often just makes the game feel incredibly bloated. Moreover, considering the story alone takes around 40+ hours to complete, the extra content just adds to an already bloated game. If I had to summarize it best, Yakuza 5 is the San Andreas of the Yakuza series: a great game that improves on its predecessor in many ways but is too ambitious for its own good. Still, even though Yakuza 5 certainly has its flaws, it's still a fantastic game that was never not enjoyable. For fans of the previous games, as long as you're willing to deal with the amount of bloat, I'd highly suggest giving Yakuza 5 a try.

I played this game on Steam Deck.
My journey across the story of Yakuza has never been more in-depth, diverse and satisfying since I first played Yakuza 0. After playing Yakuza 4, I was nearly dreading the thought of having to go through another game with not just 4 separate converging stories, but a fifth to boot. However, RGG's storytelling from 4 to 5 has an incredible jump in quality and engagement that I was on the edge of my seat from beginning to end.
The story is full of twists and turns as you would expect from this franchise. A slough of mysteries and antagonists, making you wonder how everything is connected, what brings all of these characters together.
Kiryu and Saejima have the bulk of your introduction to the story. The game is aware of the fact that your characters need quick time to level up as to not drag the story, since you have 5 characters to play with, so don;t worry about having to spend hours grinding up each character, there isnt much need for that, but it is rewarding if you put in the extra effort of course.
Haruka is the outlier of the group since she is the only character who does not fight (well, unless you count dancing as fighting), her chapter is somewhat shared with Akiyama to keep you in the habit of fighting instead of having an entire chapter allowing you to forget. Shinada finishes greetings off with perhaps the fastest chapter in the game before the story begins to converge.
Each character resides in their own city to explore, some familiar, some brand new.
Kiryu in Fukuoka, Saejima in Tsukimino, Akiyama and Haruka in Kamurocho and Sotenbori, and finally Shinada in Nagoya. Each have side stories you can progress in optionally for additional story content, personally, my favorite was Saejima's in the mountains. Theres an entire multi-hour side story there with a monstrous bear antagonizing a small village and it has a really satisfying ending if you're willing to complete it.
If I had to name one critique of the story, it would be that it tries to hard with some of its twists. Every time you think you know the true villain, someone new pops up who was seemingly behind it all (again.. and again). This does take away a bit of satisfaction from the conclusion as figuring out who the villain is is nigh impossible for the player, its something the story has to show you and explain why everything it told you previously was wrong. Dont get me wrong, the story is good, its emotional, its enticing, the climax is incredible and the final battle is unforgettable, but it would have been nice to have had less misdirection. You wont know whos behind it all until the very end, and thats unfortunate in my opinion.
All in all, I give Yakuza 5 a 9/10. Combat is the best so far, the characters are as engaging as ever, and the story, even with my nitpicks, is one youll remember.

So, another remaster, still with the old engine, but noticeably better graphics than before, an almost-usable UI (although the map is still [i]entirely[/i] underwhelming), and more, like shops taking on-line orders now, [i]LOL[/i]. You travel (and eat, drink, and, of course fight) across quite a few (fictional) parts of Japan, playing multiple characters, most of which you've probably seen before, but one of them has grown up quite a bit and sports entirely different abilities. You might guess this would be foreshadowing the 'jobs' mechanics of later episodes, but, no, it's just a collection of minigames, mostly rhythm-based. But don't worry (except about the really weird ones, 'Running Girl', [i]cough[/i]): even if you're not cut out for those, it should be... fun, actually!

Story-wise, there's a [i]lot[/i] to like, with less intrusive cutscenes than before (you can fast-forward most of the time and not just skip) and a bit more "show" than "tell", which is great, despite lore-dumps and "go talk to X then talk to Y, then talk to X again" loops definitely still being a thing. There's [i]tons[/i] to do, and even if you initially don't intend to, you may still need to travel back and forth a bit to get to a point where you're ready for the finale (it can seem like a but of a drag, but just finish the initial training master arcs in each city, gather lots of high-potency energy drinks, and you'll be fine). 

The way all the various storylines come together in the end is [i]very[/i] well done, moving even, and more than compensate for the bits that don't make all that much sense. And there's still plenty to explore after the main story concludes (as you can defer the nonessential side jobs until then), but whether you'll actually want to do that mostly depends on your tolerance for the dated environment. Despite that, easily one of the better entries in the series!

What is a game if not a mirror of life? Yakuza 5 Remastered is not simply an upgraded title—it is a sprawling, ambitious reflection of human struggle and perseverance, painted across the diverse landscapes of Japan. It is operatic in scale and yet deeply intimate. Few games have dared to go this far, and even fewer have succeeded in making every step feel meaningful.

Five protagonists. Five cities. Five personal odysseys. This is no ordinary sequel. It is a meditation on identity and purpose. Each character walks a path riddled with ghosts of the past and dreams deferred. Haruka, especially, stands out. To make a pop idol's journey as emotionally resonant as a former hitman's path to redemption? That’s bold. That’s new. That’s art.

As a person who believes that gameplay should echo the philosophy of the narrative, I was impressed by how Yakuza 5 Remastered handles tone and variety. The shift between combat, racing, dancing, and managing an idol career could be jarring in the hands of less confident developers. But Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio pulls it off with finesse. These transitions don’t feel like detours—they’re vital arteries of the game’s emotional and thematic structure.

What I admire most is the meticulous worldbuilding. Each city—Fukuoka, Sapporo, Osaka, Nagoya, and Tokyo—feels like its own character. The snow crunching under Saejima’s boots in Hokkaido. The neon pulse of Sotenbori. The modest shops tucked away in Nagoya's alleys. These are more than backdrops; they are living, breathing environments that root the drama in reality.

Technically, the remastered version sharpens the experience without losing its soul. The enhanced visuals honor the original while respecting modern standards. Frame rate improvements smoothen the pacing, but it’s the storytelling—always the storytelling—that elevates Yakuza 5 Remastered to something greater than nostalgia.

This isn’t just a game about yakuza. It’s a game about dreams. About people trying to hold onto something—honor, family, truth—in a world constantly trying to tear them apart. It is, in many ways, a game I wish I had made.

No numerical score can capture the layered beauty of this title. Like a good film or novel, it lingers in the mind long after the credits roll.

In Yakuza 5 Remastered, the fight is never just physical. It is always—always—about the heart.

Yakuza 5 is an extremely ambitious game. In so many ways, this game tries to be more than it's ilk. From the improvements to how city exploration is handled, the minutia of ways the game's combat feels better than the games that RGG Studio developed before it, to the intensity that is the ~60 hour long story it boasts. Yakuza 5 tries and in many ways succeeds at being more than its contemporaries, while stumbling along the way.

Out of the first five games in the series Yakuza 5 is the first truly modern feeling Yakuza game. Kiryu no longer turns and stops on a dime, and his movement speed has been increased to help with the general long stretches of road you have to travel in this game. Pedestrian AI is generally an improvement over the other two PS3 games, but has some very peculiar interactions which may affect your experience. Often times I found characters walking in front of the camera during cutscenes, or even thugs chewing the scenery by standing completely still and staring down my character as he acts like they're not even there. While outside of cutscenes pedestrians have AI closer to Yakuza 0, they still collide with you like in Yakuza 3 and 4 and this can be a really big problem when trying to get somewhere quickly.

Combat feels like a natural progression from Yakuza 4. Returning characters Kiryu, Saejima and Akiyama all get improvements that feels like essential parts of their moveset and each character plays around nicely with the new Climax Heat system which gives Kiryu a transformation super while Saejima gets to end his combos with grabs and Akiyama gets a launcher that sets him up for an air combo string. These are all perfect additions to the movesets these characters had in Yakuza 4, and I feel that RGG should keep and expand on these moves in future games. Series newcomer Shinada has a moveset that might be hard to get accustomed to at first, but as you level him up more and play around with him more you'll find that his mixed Grappler / Weapon Master style fits right in with the series' other protagonists. It's experimental and enjoyable even if it takes more effort to finish enemies. Him playing so differently from the other protagonists is shown best by the way his attacks are animated. He's rough, often cruel and unrefined. It's clear by watching him fight that he's a self taught grappler, which mean that his individual hits don't hit quite as hard as professionals like Kiryu and Saejima. The way Shinada fights is completely unlike any other character in the series and when you really get the hang of him, he's a whole lot of fun you can't find elsewhere.

Now it's time to discuss Yakuza 5's most controversial aspect: The Story. It starts with Kiryu trying to maintain anonymity under the fake name Taichi Suzuki and live a civilian life, while fragments of his past through the Tojo Clan are trying time and again to pull him back in. While this general plot outline could be used to summarize Yakuza 2 through Yakuza 4 before this game, what makes Yakuza 5's version of this story so special is Kiryu's attitude towards the people trying to interrupt his civilian life, and how much it feels like he's aged and grown jaded to the Tojo Clan not being able to solve their own problems. This setup is simple, it feels almost like an apology to long term fans of the series for saving Kiryu for last quarter of Yakuza 4.

The biggest problems with Yakuza 5's story come with it's pacing and how disconnected the protagonist's stories are from each other. The game starts with Kiryu in Fukuoka, but there are four other protagonists (Saejima, Haruka, Akiyama and Shinada, introduced in that order) and each character's individual story is relatively separated from each other. Saejima's story is centered on redemption, Haruka and Akiyama who share a story is focused heavily on working hard for the sake of others and acts as a critique of idol culture and Shinada's story echoes similar themes to Haruka's with him being a former baseball star while also being focused on a mystery. Each of these stories are completely separated from each other, the only through-lines being the happenings of the Tojo Clan and Omi Alliance, [spoiler]the alleged death of Goro Majima[/spoiler], and the Osakan Detective Kurosawa showing up in nearly every character's story at some point. Each character's story is a roughly ~10hr - 15hr journey, and them all being completely isolated from one another means you go 30hrs or more since you've last seen a character who ends up being widely important, then when they're brought up later you likely won't have any idea who they are. Kiryu's segment gets this the worst, because the Tojo Clan members who bother him are extremely important but his part of the story happens right away and they don't appear anywhere else in the game until the Finale where all five player characters meet up in Kamurocho. 

On the subject of Kamurocho, the finale has some issues of it's own. The biggest issues I have with the Finale of Yakuza 5 is that the big bad guys feel insignificant. This has to deal with the pacing issue I outlined in the last paragraph, but aside from that it simply feels like the big string puller has infinite power, and is able to manipulate anyone, even Kiryu: The *Dragon of Dojima* effortlessly. I don't believe for a second in the power fantasy of Yakuza 5's villain. I'm told over and over by the story about how the main characters are under his control but it all just comes across as a convenience of the script. There's a moment where four major characters are on the rooftop of Kamurocho Hills, and they're forced to fight with one another because "it's the only way to lure the mastermind out" which just leads to them all being exhausted and unable to actually stop the mastermind when he shows himself. It's as contrived as it sounds. Aside from that, the final boss fight / final series of boss fights are incredible. Kiryu's final boss is maybe the best single boss fight in the whole series up to what was released when Yakuza 5 came out, rivaling Shindo from Yakuza 2 in terms of spectacle. That being said, from starting the final segment to credits rolling can easily take you three hours. It is yet another victim of Yakuza 5's weird pacing problems that compound into this game feeling big for the sake of being big.

When all is said and done Yakuza 5 exists how it is, with all its strengths and all its flaws. It is the perfect intermediate piece for what the Yakuza series was with 1 through 4, and what the Yakuza series would become with 0 onward. A lot of it's strong ideas such as Shinada's combat style being based around weapon mastery or having a grand narrative that plays around with it's protagonists being puzzle pieces that connect the greater whole when put together are handled much more confidently in Yakuza 0 and I don't think that Yakuza 0 would've been as good as it is without RGG being able to see Yakuza 5's shortcomings. Yakuza 5 ran so Yakuza 0 could walk. 

Your enjoyment of Yakuza 5 hinges entirely on how much you can appreciate it as an interesting and flawed intermediate piece to Yakuza's history. For me, I respect that enough to really enjoy this game in spite of it's significant story flaws and how long the game is.

Yakuza 5 is leaps and bounds beyond 3 and 4. It feels a whole LOT closer to Yakuza 0 and Kiwami 1 than the older ones. The story tries to build on the older games. I often see Yakuza 5 at the bottom of people's lists of their favourite games in the franchise, and I can absolutely understand where some people may take major issue with this entry. Most prominently is the length. Yakuza 0, which in the modern day is many people's entry point to the series, is the only similarly long game up to this point, but it is pretty evenly split between the two protagonists, each with three fighting styles and bespoke side activities that span 80% of the runtime (Real Estate for Kiryu and Cabaret for Majima). Yak5 steps up the ambitions of Yak4 by swapping Tanimura out for Shinada, and then adding Kiryu's daughter in as a playable J-Pop idol for a not-insignificant portion of the game. 

The forced tonal and pacing whiplash of the Haruka sections, while significantly more fun and involved, reminded me of my least favourite necessary evil of Yak3 - the orphanage sections. Being forced to play an entirely different management sim in the middle of my beat em up action game was jarring in both instances, but RGG has at least learned from the feedback to Yak3 by allowing a lot more player freedom in their approach to handling Haruka's rise to fame. However, repeat playthroughs would definitely strain even my patience for the tedium of checking handshake events, TV interviews and dance battles off the ever growing list when I could instead by unravelling possible the most complex Yakuza plot to date. 

The story in this entry is, without a doubt, incredibly well handled for how many moving parts it has, and how much of it is obscured for at least 40 hours of runtime. Without spoiling too much, Yakuza 5 addresses the clear flaws that have developed in the management of both the Tojo and the Omi clans over the course of the last 5 games, with power vacuums of all kinds being formed in the wake of powerhouses like Kiryu, Saejima and Ryuji Goda. It all comes to a head in the final 2 hours of gameplay, as has become standard, with in my opinion one or two too many twists pulled off at the last minute. One major character is given a backstory no one expected, especially given their role in Yak0, but through careful headcanon I have managed to move forward, inconsistencies abated. 

Another lesson learned, this time from Yak4 was to put Kiryu as the first player character, in a brand new location. Same-same really, Kiryu is angry at the situation in which he finds himself to allow Haruka to pursue her dreams, but accepts that keeping his kids safe is the priority. The taxi driving/racing segments were surprisingly fun, and Nagasugai in the city of Fukuoka was a perfectly acceptable first city to explore. 

Saejima continues his trend from Yak4 for having the absolute WORST pacing to start his otherwise awesome gameplay. Another fucking prison section, with admittedly a FAR better overall storyline and concluding fight. Between his inevitable prison break and winding up at the next new map set in Sapporo, Saejima has to face the forces of the Hokkaido mountains, where gods and beasts alike challenge what stands as my favourite playstyle in terms of Heat Actions since Majima's Breaker in Yak0 - their brutality is unmatched. Tsukimino itself is nothing too special, and I spent very little time there - I genuinely can't even remember a general layout, as much of Saejima's more fun sections are based in his final sections in the area and where I am running wildly through the streets, or in the mountains, with a shotgun in hand. 

Haruka brings us back to Osaka's good ol' Sotenbori, a favourite only rivalled by Kamurocho in terms of utilisation across the games. As the home turf of the Omi clan, it only makes sense that this deeply clan war-based story would feature this city, so much so that Akiyama's plotline is ALSO based here. By Chapter 2 of Haruka's section, she has met with Uncle Aki and both are investigating a mysterious murder alongside fostering Haruka's burgeoning J-Pop career. The fun of fighting as Akiyama with his rapid kicks, flawlessly choreographed was exactly what I needed after Saejima's slow brutality and alongside Haruka's measured, beat-based "combat" sections. Now, to be entirely honest, I can see myself hating being FORCED to repeat the Haruka sections if I ever had to do them again. BUT for my first time playthrough I 100%ed her entire roster, fought every street battler, and maxed out almost all my stats. I genuinely and thouroughly enjoyed the direction in which they took her character and her gameplay, and I appreciate how integrated she ended up being to the overall much darker plot. As I stated earlier this is, to my mind, a far better executed and fleshed out version of the orphanage sections of Yak3. They both serve their purpose to the overall emotional investment in Kiryu's family by the end of the game, but by allowing the player to BE Kiryu's family, while they come to terms with that fact, rather than just be shown how the children react to his life lessons was far more effective from a narrative point of view. 

Shinada really drew the short end of the stick to start with. The only brand new protagonist, in a new city (Kineicho, Nagoya), entirely unrelated to any other series leads with an, at first glace, completely surface level character motivation and plotline that did not tie back to the main narrative at all. All that, and he was the FINAL character to be introduced before the endgame. In an ironic twist, like his actual narrative, he was set up to fail, but knocked it out of the fucking park. Shinada's fighting style, while not my favourite, certainly had it's merits, and I didn't even bother to fully max him out and equip him with other weapons. Even severely depowered, he was very fun and engaging to play as. Eventually, Shinada does get wrapped up in the main plot, from several unlikely sources, and holds his own alongside legends like Kiryu and Saejima. His batting and chicken racing minigames did not interest me, so not having to complete side objectives I did not enjoy certainly improved his standing with me as an addition to an already stacked roster. 

The final act of the game saw a surprisingly complex web of backstabbing, spying, lying and powerstruggling brought to a head in an actual cohesive manner. The feeling of an actual unravelling mystery was greatly improved by my guide through the series genuinely not remembering large portions of the game, so the plot was a mystery even to him. Theory crafting as a duo was a very rewarding experience as more threads were pulled and stitched together. 

Overall, Yakuza 5 took Yak4's ambition and detail-dense plot and iterated both to hitherto unforeseen heights. Behind Yakuza 0, Yak 5 has become by second favourite game in the franchise. Kiwami 2 was prettier, but Yak 5 has three of my favourite characters in the entire franchise, fleshed out and playable for over 80 hours of game time. As the final game in this engine, I could not have asked for a better send off.

Se existe uma epopeia moderna nos videogames, esse game é Yakuza 5.

As ideias que não deram certo no quarto game voltam aqui com um aprimoramento massivo, são cinco protagonistas jogáveis, cinco narrativas que se interlaçam no decorrer de 70 horas de jogo. A qualidade aqui é impressionante: cada protagonista tem seus arcos secundários, coadjuvantes memoráveis, substories intrigantes e minigames variados. É espantosa a profundidade que encontramos em Y5, e fica bem evidente como esse jogo é o responsável por criar as fundações que tornaram Yakuza 0 tão popular.

A narrativa é a mais impactante desde o segundo jogo, principalmente porque ela realmente avança o status quo das organizações e desenvolve os personagens e suas motivações; ninguém termina Y5 da mesma forma que começa, e isso vale para praticamente todo mundo relevante. Saejima tem muito tempo para brilhar e mostrar as suas qualidades, Akiyama segue brilhando após sua estreia em Y4, Haruka passa por um grande arco e até mesmo o novato, Shinada, se destaca.

Mas em especial, preciso dizer: Kiryu é MONSTRUOSO em Yakuza 5. De longe é uma das melhores performances de um protagonista na história dos videogames, e não afirmo isso de forma leviana. O Dragão de Dojima entrega tudo nesse jogo, seus ideiais, suas inseguranças, seus sacrifícios e esperanças estão todos escancarados, e a história vai revelando isso de forma muito natural com o desenrolar dos eventos. É algo muito impressionante.

Apesar disso,o conflito principal está longe de ser perfeito, é muito dependente de plot twists e eventos convenientes para prosseguir, sem falar em algumas coisas extremamente dramáticas que ocorrem - bem pastelão, estilo novela - mas tudo fica aceitável se você não questionar muito. Nesse sentido, acho que Y0 continua a melhor história da franquia, ao menos é a melhor contada, mas não se deixe enganar, Y5 figura no Top 3 da série.

Ah, Yakuza 5...

“What if we made Yakuza 4 but cranked every dial up to 11 and also made you do a rhythm game for hours?” It’s ambitious, it’s ridiculous, and at times, it makes as much sense as Majima in a construction hat. And yet, somehow, it still slaps harder than Ryuji Goda’s final punch.

First off, let’s talk about the story—because gyatt damn there’s a lot of it. We’ve got five protagonists, five cities, and more plot twists than Nishiki’s emotional state in Kiwami. [spoiler]Kiryu, the ultimate dad and part-time taxi driver, is still trying to live a quiet life, but the yakuza have a sixth sense for ruining his peace. Saejima is back, which means another prison escape—because he apparently has a punch card for these at this point. Akiyama is here doing his usual “I have money and don’t give a damn” routine, and then we get two wildcards: Shinada, a disgraced ex-baseball player with all the debt of a college student, and Haruka, Kiryu’s adoptive daughter, who trades street fights for dance battles in her quest to become an idol.[/spoiler]

Yeah, you heard that right. In a franchise where men regularly settle disputes by pile-driving each other into concrete, you now have to progress the game through the power of synchronized choreography. And honestly? It works. Haruka’s section is like a fever dream, but compared to Yakuza 3’s orphanage chores, I’d rather be forced into an impromptu TV interview than help another kid find their lost toy.

Now, the gameplay. Yakuza 5 looked at Yakuza 3’s combat and said, “What if we didn’t make enemies block 90% of the time?” The result? Fighting actually feels good again. Each character has their own distinct playstyle: Kiryu is the classic wrecking ball of justice, Saejima hits like a truck full of bears, Akiyama’s kicks are smoother than his loans, Shinada flails around like a drunk who just learned how to throw a punch, and Haruka... well, she doesn’t fight, but she can outdance your ass.

And let’s not forget the side content, because RGG Studios went absolutely off the rails. You can be a taxi driver and literally obey the speed limit. You can bet your hard-earned yen on chicken racing. You can even go hunting in the mountains—because why wouldn’t this game have a hunting simulator crammed into it?

But let’s be real: Yakuza 5 is an absolute mess. It’s bloated, it’s all over the place, and the pacing makes Yakuza 3’s mid-game look concise. But it’s a glorious mess. By the time you reach the end, with all the betrayals, dramatic monologues, and final fights that go way too hard, you realize that this game may be a clusterfuck—but it’s our clusterfuck.

A little too long, a little too chaotic, but just like Majima, you love it anyway.

Yakuza 5 expands on the multi-protagonist approach of its predecessor, this time featuring five playable characters: Kiryu, Saejima, Akiyama, Haruka, and Shinada. Each character has their own storyline, which eventually ties into the bigger picture. 

Story:

The narrative takes some questionable turns. Kiryu leaving the orphanage felt out of character, even if it was "necessary," and his stint as a taxi driver didn’t really suit him. Saejima’s story starts off with another prison sequence (which felt like a rehash of Yakuza 4), but his survival story in the mountains was fantastic—I wish they had focused more on that instead.

Haruka’s storyline, which introduces her as a playable character, was a fresh idea but could have been done better. Akiyama, unfortunately, felt like an afterthought. Shinada, on the other hand, had the strongest arc, with an interesting baseball backstory that connected well with Dojima.

The finale had a few twists—Kurosawa being the Omi chairman instead of a detective was decent, and Aizawa being his son. But overall, the villains felt underwhelming, and the story didn't live up to its full potential. Especially compared to say Yakuza 2 and 3.

Gameplay:
Combat remains largely unchanged from Yakuza 4. Each character has their own strengths—Kiryu and Saejima are the powerhouses, Akiyama is fast, and Shinada relies on weapons. Regular enemies are easy, even on Legend difficulty, but the coliseum is another story.

The coliseum fights are tedious, with enemies blocking almost everything, having multiple health bars, and  reducing your heat action damage. Instead of being challenging, they’re just drawn-out and grindy. Some characters, like Kiryu and Saejima, can exploit certain moves to win, while Shinada struggles because he isn’t built for these fights and you can't even use weapons with him. The rewards aren’t worth the effort unless you're aiming for 100% completion. 

Side Content:
The side jobs were some of the best parts of the game. Kiryu’s taxi missions were surprisingly fun, and Saejima’s hunting segments were excellent, they should have focused his story more on that. Haruka’s idol career was interesting (even if repetitive) and something new for the series. Akiyama, unfortunately, had no job-related activities, while Shinada’s baseball minigames fit his character well. 

Minigames are the usual mix of returning and new activities. The worst one remains fishing—river fishing is okay, but sea fishing is pure frustration, thanks to the constant fishing of steel barrels. Casino and card games are trivialized by cheat items, while SEGA games are only challenging until you figure out their exploits. On the bright side, the UFO catcher was the easiest in the series—finally, no frustration there.

Bugs:
I encountered a few technical issues. The game occasionally froze when getting a weapon revelation, which made me stop doing them altogether (not that they were worthwhile). Another annoyance was the prize ticket system—despite having a “good day” status, I kept getting pocket tissues, forcing me to reload 12 times just to get a pearl. The gacha mechanics in this game were frustrating, and I hope they removed them in later entries. The game is supposed to be fun not a chore.

Conclusion
Despite its flaws, Yakuza 5 is still a great game, as my 150+ hours prove. However, it could have been better with a tighter story, improved combat balancing, and fewer grindy elements. If you're a Yakuza fan, it's worth playing, but be prepared for some frustrating moments along the way.

It didn't help that each playable character took place in a completely different city so the story overall felt very split as they would explain the character first and what they are going through before getting back into the main story of the game. The main villain was also not that great, we've had much better.

The game has you starting off with Kiryu in Fukuoka which I think was a good choice from the previous game where you played him last. At the beginning of the game however, they make you do all these different things while teaching and showing you all the different stuff you can do to the point where if you dive deep into the side stories and sub-stories, you might forget completely that something is going on in the main quest. Kiryus gameplay was fun as he is such a solid fighter with the addition of new moves you can pull such as grabbing enemies when you finish a combo and overall the most balanced character. His side stories were pretty fun too as it has you driving a taxi and I really enjoyed the ones that had you racing against other opponents. The normal taxi missions though could have gone with having less of them as most of them were just you doing multiple choice questions from dialogue, so it got repetitive. If anything they should of cut the number of Taxi missions by half.

Right after you're done with Kiryu you go to Saejima which starts exactly the same as it did with the last game, and then the same cycle repeats with him as it did with Kiryu. Saejima combat wise is improved, he is still a heavy hitter that does a ton of damage with a wider range of move sets to your disposal, especially if you level him up and learn new abilities from your master trainer. His side story was one of the most enjoyable to me as you get to go out and hunt animals by being strategic as you need to be quiet when approaching a deer or with Bears being able to dodge your bullet which adds tension and forces you to land the perfect shot. My only complaint is that walking was pretty slow and the animation to set up traps and take them off got annoying as it dragged. Saejima was also the only character where you had 2 different places to travel to as the hunting side stories took place in a small village while everything else took place in the main City of Sapporo.

After you're done with Saejima you get to play... Get this... HARUKA! Which was completely different from all the other characters gameplay-wise. Haruka Does not fight but instead engages in dance battles which has you playing a rhythm game similar to karaoke. All of her side stories events are about the same thing with the exception of some where it does the same multiple choice questions you had to do with Kiryu and another one where you shake hands and answer questions while timing how long to hold the hand. As much as I appreciated Harukas part of the game, I think it dragged on for far too long because all the side stories were the same thing repeated 5 times over to the point where trying to complete it just felt like a menial task more than a fun quirky gimmick. I'm not sure why they gave Haruka the most side stories, but the game would of benefited if they just slashed that number by half just like Kiryus.

Akiyama Starts in the middle of Harukas chapter and I was actually relieved that he was the only character that didn't get side stories, you still have sub stories though and those were fine. Akiyama to me was probably the most fun character to play. He's quick, snappy with his kicks and they gave him a new ability where you can throw people in the air and whale on them. Akiyama felt like the closest thing to Dante from DMC being in this game. Him and Haruka also take place in Dotonbori so no new city for him which was honestly a relief as well.

Finally, the last character you play is a washed out Baseball Pro named Shinada. Out of all of the character's story and even the main Story of the game, I enjoyed his the most. I felt like he was relatable and felt bad for him a lot of the times because of his past and what he had to go through, there was also other times where I just felt like he was a complete idiot that doesn't have any common sense. His combat style was my least favorite, I did not like playing him and I did not like going through his section of the game because I just really did not enjoy how he fought. They advertise the character as a Weapon user but he's actually more of a Grappler and his way of fighting is just very odd. His Side stories were pretty enjoyable though as all it has you do is play in the batting cages, so if you like baseball you will like his Side stories. With his Part of the game they also introduced the best Character in all of the Franchise, Koichi Takasugi. I love that guy, he made me laugh a couple of times.

After you're done with everyone's story, the game throws you back in Kamurocho (Finally!) for the final chapter, and man do I love Kamurocho, I wish the game would just let you play there from the start instead of having you go on this wild goose chase collecting members. So besides the combat for each individual Character, I feel like This game also suffered from the same thing that Yakuza 3 suffered where enemies would just constantly block all the time, Blockuza was very apparent and alive in this entry. Normal Enemies wouldn't block as often but it still happened enough for me to notice and Boss fights... They all just blocked almost always. I don't understand what happened, Not sure if its a remaster issue or what but it was incredibly annoying fighting bosses at times, all I could do most of the time was just grab and throw them. Speaking of bosses, a lot of them were very poorly designed as some that I would fight would Spam the same move constantly without having any sort of variety. Enemies across the city would also spawn on top of each other and there were too many all over the place as I would often get into an encounter, finish it and somehow get right into another one because the enemy would be right on me. I realized that this had something to do with a text you get daily about your luck being bad or good, and if it was bad, enemies would spawn more often across the city.

Overall Was the game fun? Yeah, it was pretty fun, just too many things to do.

Yakuza 5 is an interesting entry to the franchise, as it is the biggest game in the series in terms of sheer content, at least as far as I'm concerned (haven't played 7 or 8 yet). This has its upsides and downsides, so we'll start with the bad. 

The combat styles aren't evolved much from the previous game, introducing mostly half baked mechanics like the climax heat, which manifests itself differently depending on the character, but you can tell, especially for kiryu and akiyama, that it isn't fully fleshed out and is mostly a simple addition to the arsenal. Also, generally speaking the game feels rather easy, which to be fair is a problem with Y4 as well, but considering how busted Kiryu and even Saejima are this game... yeah.

The story can be a bit of a convoluted mess, since it tries to balance 5 different storylines which don't have much overlap until the later chapters in the game, so there's a lot to keep track of and it can definitely feel overwhelming on a first run.

On the other hand, the side content in this game is probably the best in the series. Each character has their own unique piece of side content with its own story, from taxi driving, to animal hunting and baseball, Yakuza 5 has it all and it still keeps the minigames from the previous titles that we all love. It also features 5 unique cities, and the only playable version of Haruka, which is awesome and a joy to see. 

Despite the storyline being a bit of a mess, it still wraps up incredibly well in the end, even when considering how the final boss is a pretty big question mark moment (who is also, mechanically speaking, the best boss fight in the series up to this point). Shinada's unique storyline is also one of the best in the series, up there with something like Majima's in Y0, it's a shame that the character doesn't really return in future installments, as it often happens with these games,  

All in all, Yakuza 5 is most likely the best out of the first 5 titles, showing the consistent growth of the franchise, and is definitely a game that won't happen ever again, considering it's ridiculous size. There's a reason why this one's a fan favorite.

The good stuff on Yakuza 5:

1) Most playable characters in one game the series, which adds a lot fighting style diversity (and Haruka's DDR mini-game pseudo combat style). Also the most cities in a Yakuza game, which makes the scope feel appropriately grand and the virtual tourism element really adventurous.
2) Goes without saying, but it's a Yakuza game, so it's hilarious and exciting and wild and fun all at once.
3) Some of the best "medium sized" mini-games in the series in the Initial D style racing, the Taxi driving game, and the Cabela's Big Game Hunting game with most of the best smaller mini-games that show up regularly.
4) Shinada is the best "one and done" character in the whole series, making a strong impression here and then bouncing out of the series forever. Shine on you crazy Baseball Boy!
5) Obviously arguable, but I think this IS the best Yakuza soundtrack, which is a very high bar to clear. I love other individual songs from other games better, but in terms of totality I probably listen to the Y5 soundtrack the most overall. Some fire tracks here!

The Bad:
1) The game's best chapters are the 1st and the 4th by FAR, which means the games middle drags a LOT and it kind of ends on a bit of a whimper. They frontload too much of the best stuff in this one and should've pace it out a bit more.
2) Saejima goes to prison only to break out AGAIN like in Y4 and it just . . . he still has half his chapter to go through so this whole sequence really feels like them trying to do the same sequence from Y4 again but better, which it is, but its a HUGE retread, and feels tacked on since his role in the plot is less critical. 
3) Haruka's segment is VERY divisive. I think it's a great change of pace for the game, but a lot of people hate it, and frankly, yeah I can get it. Also even though you CAN fail her Idol gameshow contest, it doesn't matter due to the larger plot, so it's all a bit of fake tension really. They also aren't *really* delving too much into the idol lifestyle in as critical way as you might expect. Perfect Blue this ain't. 
4) Akiyama is a great returning character from Y4 but his potential is wasted here. More so in Y6, but this starts the trend.
5) Man this ending. It's just . . . THE most convoluted nonsense. Even for a Yakuza game. But the real problem is the final boss . . . they go for a twist boss here and it just does not work well. There's way too much pathos and hype for the fight going into it considering who it ends up being, so even though it is a cool fight, it just seems very unjustified. 

All that said, again, this IS a Yakuza game. It's great overall. I wouldn't recommend anyone start with 5 at all, it's way too embedded in the series lore to really work as a 1st game in my opinion, but even with some of its worst bits it holds up as probably the 2nd or 3rd best in the main Kiryu series (after Zero and 6 IMO).

Yakuza 5 my beloved.

You get to play as Kiryu, Saejima, Haruka, Akiyama, and Shinada.
All five were absolutely fun to play as.  Each having their own side stories.

On my first playthrough alone, I clocked in 88 hours, which was far longer than the 67 hours I did on my first playthrough on Yakuza 0.  And honestly, the sidestories were probably the reason I stayed so long, just as it was for 0.

Kiryu's at a debatable strongest here, as your bounding throws are completely free, Tiger Drop actually negates all damage through the ENTIRE animation, both attack and rewind.  And, you can negate all damage yourself by just entering dragons rage.

Saejima's still fun to play as and is great for crowd work. However, Tsukimino has a slightly minor problem where the map is so constricted that you'll likely fight a guy right as you get out of one fight.  I didn't have a problem with that though.  And, you can take a picture of Miku in there.

Haruka gets to be playable in game, basing it off as rhythm as she's now an Idol.  Doing various dance battles and the like.  And her music soundtrack is great.  It's got the songs that I'm willing to listen to outside of the game, among other ones.

Akiyama, he's still fun to play as.  He's got his kicks, and you can even do air combos with him.
Some people might say that having an air combo which apparently misses half the time was a waste on Akiyama, but I never had that problem.  He's either good, or he gets his ass kicked in by the Komaki duo.  

Shinada my beloved.  You get to have a baseball sidestory that is my personal favorite in here, rivaling that of Kiryu's Taxi Racing.  His combat is my favorite in the game, going above Kiryu simply because of "My Meteor Tackle" and his own version of a bounding throw.  He can get into grabs in multiple ways, and he's really good with weapons.
Continuing on that, some people say his weapons aren't very good, that being the sturdy metal pole, long pole, knife, and katana.        And to that, I say that you really shouldn't soley rely on his weapons.
Shinada already is great at fighting if you know how to use his overflowing amount of I-Frames.    I personally only pulled out weapons if I wanted to utilize the increased XP on enemy finish, or if I needed it as a solution to an enemy.  Just, don't be stupid with them and you'll get your use from them.


The story's fun, it has a lot of twists and turns, and the final boss has a lot of health, which I find to be refreshing.

But most importantly, Baka Mitai was introduced as a karaoke track for the first time in 5.   There's also Machine Gun Kiss, which is also amazing.

Anyways, Yakuza 5's a great game.  I'll be moving on to playing Isshin before I play 6.

Pros:

- This game is PACKED. You play as FIVE different people throughout the game, across FIVE different places in Japan. Aside from Kamurocho, you get to go to Fukuoka, Hokkaido, Osaka, and Nagoya. Each of these characters have their own sub-stories and side missions. There is a boatload of mini-games and other stuff to discover. It literally has a little something for everyone.
- Just like in the previous game, the switching between characters is easy to do in the final chapter and the different fighting styles of each character are still just as good to experiment with.
- After the combat system of Y3 and Y4, this one feels the most fun to play with. It’s on the same game engine as Yakuza 0 and Yakuza Kiwami which I’ve praised for the solid combat. You can see the seeds of greatness being cultivated in this game.
- Haruka’s journey to becoming a pop idol is my favorite storyline. Handshake events, dance battles, rivals being bullies, etc. All the good shit is here. “So Much More” is my jam now and forever.
- YOU CAN CHOOSE TO FIGHT KIRYU. Just like in Y4, the plot somehow leads to you getting the chance to fight the Dragon of Dojima himself. It’s an optional choice, but it is still a very cool moment.
- But honestly, the sheer amount of content in this game is crazy. It’s like no one told the developers “NO” when they were pitching ideas. Rhythm game? Yes. Taxi Driving game? Yes. Racing game? Yes. Shooting game? Yes. Dating Sim? Yes. Baseball game? There’s two types! Air Hockey with a beautiful girl? Yes. Cooking ramen noodles? Hell yeah. The only thing it’s missing is the cabaret club management and this would’ve been my favorite Yakuza game of all time.
- The plot is actually pretty interesting. The payoff with the villain at the end is a little weak, but where Yakuza shines is not in making sense, but in making hype. And hype up every single fight it does.

Cons:

- It’s not Yakuza if its greatest strength is also its greatest weakness. This series isn’t for everyone, and even this game isn’t for every Yakuza fan. Having to keep jumping between characters can be a bit jarring and just like in Y4, switching to a low-level character after having just maxed out a previous one can be a bit jarring since most of the moves are level-locked.
- The leveling system is horrendous. You’re capped off at level 20 which you can achieve easily, but then you have to pass an insanely difficult combat challenge to increase the cap to level 25 (per character). But thankfully, the game included an easier way to achieve soul orbs (ability points) with the IF8 mini-game.
- Some parts of the story can get a bit dragging, even for Yakuza standards. Since most of the side-stories are required, it can be distracting and you will end up forgetting the plot if you don’t pay attention well enough. There were times that I had to google who the character on the screen was because I had completely forgotten about them.
- Because of the amount of content, completionists are either going to love this game or hate it. This is the only Yakuza game where I didn’t bother with Haruka’s Requests or eating all the meals in all the restaurants. There were just too many.
