Yakuza 5 is the biggest game in the series so far. Five protagonists, five arcs, five cities—it’s ambitious, and mostly pays off, though the scope sometimes overwhelms.

[b]Gameplay[/b]  
Kiryu doesn’t change much mechanically, but he didn’t need to. Dragon Spirit turns him into a monster while draining Heat, and the new grab-after-finisher mechanic opens damage loops, making his kit more versatile. Tiger Drop is still here, but he’s just fun to play without relying on it. He remains the reliable all-rounder, and his combat is at its best here.

Akiyama is similar to Yakuza 4: fast, flashy, all about kicks. Launch Strike lets him juggle enemies, though it burns Heat and can be dodged mid-air, limiting its usefulness. Heat Actions are still situational, so you’ll repeat a few, though there’s slightly more variety than in 4. Fun, but comparatively plain.

Saejima finally got the glow-up he needed. In 4 he was clunky, but in 5 he feels like the powerhouse he was always meant to be. Heat grants hyper armor, and Tiger Puppetry—grabbing enemies and flailing them around—is effective and satisfying. Unique Weapon grabs can one-shot regular thugs in his city. Charge moves are rewarding now thanks to guard break. Easily one of the series’ biggest improvements.

Shinada’s combat feels unfinished. Three-hit combos cripple his Armor Break, his “weapon guy” gimmick is underwhelming, and Meteor Tackle rarely works on bosses. Most fights involve spamming basic combos or grabs. Not unplayable, but disappointing compared to the rest.

Haruka doesn’t fight, but her rhythm game arc is enjoyable. Songs are fun, mechanics simple, and it’s a nice break. She can be a bit of an airhead, and the game portrays her as almost unrealistically good, but her kindness carries the section.

[b]Story[/b]  
The story is fine—probably the best word for it. It’s an upgrade over Yakuza 4 (and 1 and 2), but weaker than 3. Pacing is rough, and some arcs wander.

[b]MAJOR SPOILERS AHEAD[/b]

Kiryu’s arc is the strongest and sets everything in motion. He works as a taxi driver to [spoiler] support the orphanage from afar, creating a new identity while staying involved[/spoiler]. The showdown with [spoiler]the Tojo Clan[/spoiler] is a perfect opening—spectacle, drama, and a reminder of why Kiryu drives the series. It sets up the [spoiler]Tojo-Omi conflict[/spoiler] and propels the story naturally.

Saejima’s arc is the weakest again. [spoiler]Prison feels like lazy setup, and the sequence is too short to matter[/spoiler]. His [spoiler]snowy village segment[/spoiler] is more enjoyable thanks to [spoiler]hunting[/spoiler] gameplay, but narratively underwhelming.

Haruka’s arc digs into why Kiryu is [spoiler]a civilian[/spoiler] and her struggles as an idol. Park treats her [spoiler]terribly early on, and the redemption doesn’t fully erase that[/spoiler], but Haruka’s strength and kindness carry her story, adding emotional stakes that amplify Kiryu’s sacrifices.

Akiyama’s arc is short but solid. [spoiler]Detective[/spoiler] work isn’t a perfect fit, but his charisma works. It bridges Haruka’s idol world with the [spoiler]criminal underworld[/spoiler], though his role could’ve been expanded given his limited spotlight.

Shinada’s arc, on the other hand, is probably the most enjoyable on its own. It’s disconnected from the main story—cut entirely, and the larger plot wouldn’t change—but as a standalone tale, it’s fantastic. Shinada feels the most human protagonist: flawed, selfish, but grounded. His struggles with failure, shame, and redemption are compelling. Koichi Takasugi, his moneylender and [spoiler]only fan[/spoiler], elevates it further, giving warmth and authenticity missing from other arcs, definitely one of the best characters in the entire series despite being only a supporting one.

The finale tries to pull everything together, but it doesn’t fully land. [spoiler]Baba’s betrayals[/spoiler] drag on, losing impact. [spoiler]Masaru Watase[/spoiler] is underutilized, more cameo than pivotal. Park’s connection to [spoiler]Majima[/spoiler] is dropped entirely, wasting potential to tie Haruka’s arc to the larger story.

Final boss fights are mixed. [spoiler]Shinada vs. Baba[/spoiler] is weak—the endless [spoiler]betrayals[/spoiler] killed tension plus they never really interacted before that point. [spoiler]Saejima vs. Majima[/spoiler] should’ve been massive, but lacks buildup; fun mechanically, but feels like fanservice which honestly at least it does pretty well. [spoiler]Akiyama vs. Kanai[/spoiler] works in the moment but leaves little impression.

[spoiler]Kiryu vs. Aizawa[/spoiler] is the spectacle highlight—flashy, intense, mechanically one of the best fights in the series. But as a climax, it feels hollow; [spoiler]Aizawa[/spoiler] lacks emotional connection, just serving as the last obstacle.

By the credits, the finale feels stitched together rather than earned. Five arcs promised a massive payoff, but deliver loosely connected fights and half-resolved storylines. Impressive superficially, but the cracks show on reflection.

[b]Side Content[/b]  
Finally let's talk about side-content, this is where Yakuza 5 goes overboard. Tons of minigames, substories, and activities for each character—[spoiler]hunting[/spoiler], taxi driving, baseball, dance battles—making it the most varied entry. Casually, it’s a blast.

100% completion, however, is brutal. Food and drink lists are repetitive across cities, the Coliseum grind is tedious (defeat roaming contestants to spawn minibosses, rank up each character), and other tasks, like batting centers for gravure pictures, feel like padding.

Casually, the side content is the best in the series. Completionist play is some of the worst.

[b]TL;DR: Yakuza 5 is massive, messy, and ambitious. Combat is at its best, Shinada’s arc shines individually, and Saejima is finally fun to play. Story starts strong with Kiryu but gradually goes downhill, and the finale is more scale than payoff. The completion list will frustrate, but sticking to main arcs and side content at your own pace makes it one of the series’ most enjoyable games.[/b]

The core idea of Yakuza 5, four parts in four different cities, along with a whole slew of new minigames easily made it the most ambitious game in the series up to that point. In addition to all that, the game received a large overhaul in the areas of lighting and gameplay. It still feels pretty similar to Yakuza 4, but you also start to see the beginnings of 0 - it is more or less a halfway point. The lighting alone really gives the game a face-lift that makes it resemble what would later be 0 more than any of the previous titles. It also includes some new gameplay mechanics in combat: the additions of enemy reinforcements, enemies that run away and crowds that back up as you approach, opening the combat area up a little more. It also introduced Climax Heat Actions and AppStims that newcomers to the franchise may recognize from the Kiwami games (though there the former works more like red heat from Y3-4). A more unfortunate change to the gameplay is that weapons now have requirements to equip them; you increase your weapon ability by using weapons you pick up. Possibly the worst change of all, though, is how they handle Premium Adventure and NG+ in this entry. Unlike every mainline entry before and after, you cannot create clear data in Premium Adventure. This means that if you do NG+, nothing you do in Premium Adventure will matter for it. This idiotic system premiered in Kurohyou: Ryu Ga Gotoku Shinsen for the PSP and went on to be in the original Ishin release (but fixed for the remake). 

The music in Yakuza 5 is some of the best in the series up to this point with some truly great tracks that hype you up for the action and make the emotional moments even more memorable. The substories as well overall are particularly strong, though, unfortunately, these don't escape the iffy issues that the series sometimes falls into and in my opinion, they are particularly bad here as well being more prolonged than usual such as an entire substory about a mixer where the entire joke is “haha they're ugly aren't they” and another substory where the joke is essentially that they're fat. There's also a substory that's rather copaganda with an ending that's somewhat jarring. 

Another thing that really stood out to me is the sheer variety - and not only in terms of the four cities. It seemed to me the NPCs had more variety to them, between the random civilians to enemies. There's also quite a few unique locations in the main story and even substories. 

One negative thing about the game's story is that it has some fairly bad pacing problems. For the most part each individual part is fine but the end of each one is something of a cliffhanger and the plot is really put on hold to introduce each character’s storyline. However, the way the plot is laid out I'm not sure how they could have rectified this other than alternating characters every chapter or two and that could get messy fast with the amount of protagonists in this one. 

Part 1 starts off with… Kiryu? But why is he a taxi driver in Fukuoka? Why isn't he with Haruka? This game really likes its mysteries and you're hit with multiple right off the bat. Kiryu’s taxi minigames are very fun, especially when you start street racing to some really hype eurobeat. 

Part 2 is with Saejima and his part is… Decidedly rougher. His part doesn't really open up much at all until chapter 3 with his side story minigame and even then, he doesn't get his substories until chapter 4. The way his story is handled is baffling and really kills all momentum the plot had, unfortunately. The first two chapters are mainly cutscenes and dialogue but if you stick with it there is atleast good payoff on those chapters. Once things open up it becomes very enjoyable. 

Part 3 is very unique for the franchise - it features Haruka, now turned idol and has two different rhythm games and a multitude of other minigames as part of her career. It portrays some unfortunate truths about the idol industry that can be quite uncomfortable, particularly early on but I do think it’s important that they didn’t try to brush it under the rug. Partway through her part, Akiyama becomes playable, his story intertwining with that of Haruka’s and creating a really lovely dynamic for them. If Kiryu is her father, then Akiyama is like her uncle. New to this game for Akiyama’s moveset as well are some ridiculous juggling mechanics that allows him to do some Devil May Cry-esque float-y attacks. This part has the strongest set of characters in the game, in my opinion.

Part 4 features a new protagonist by the name of Tatsuo Shinada who is a broke ex-pro Baseball player turned nightlife journalist. He is a very charming and likable, down to earth guy even to the local bartenders of Kineicho, Nagoya. His moveset is very weapon oriented, with an unbreakable pipe that only does a little bit of damage. He later gets access to a master who will help increase weapon durability, as well. 

On the whole I enjoyed the story but unfortunately the story crumbles a bit at the end for me. The reveal of the final boss in particular feels like a massive asspull that actively made it worse for me.

I'm considering suing SEGA for emotional damage for that ending, but I guess I can forgive them since they put more rhythm games in my rhythm game and they introduced my goat Shinada. In typical Yakuza fashion, this game was peak, though I wish Kiryu was allowed to be happy for once instead of being taken out back and shot emotionally at the beginning of every game. 9/10 would Yakuza 5 again (I docked them a point for not letting me perform the final song as Haruka).

[h2]This has to be one of the [i]hardest[/i] "recommended" ratings I'm leaving on this platform.[/h2]
As far as Yakuza games go, this has both some of the [i]highest[/i] and the [i]lowest[/i] points in the entire franchise.
And it's [b]too much videogame for its own good.[/b]

It's easily the LONGEST Yakuza game, and the one with the most playable characters and places to visit [b]by far[/b], split into 5 characters across 5 towns. And the side content [i]matches[/i] that length.
Every character has anywhere from 15 to 20 substories. There's more minigames than ever. There's THREE sets of "locker keys" to collect across dfiferent towns, plus even [i]more[/i] extra collectibles outside of that.
Every character has a SIDE STORY that's like a mega-substory centered around a unique minigame that only that character can do. Think the cabaret/real estate stuff from Zero, but [b]five of them[/b].

This philosophy of [i]"fuck it do as much stuff as possible"[/i] kinda spreads throughout the entire game.
[b]The first and fourth chapters have easily some of the strongest storytelling in the series, and could've EASILY been their own games/spinoffs as-is.
Everything else is basically the opposite, and the way the story and characters come together by the end is about as messy as in Yakuza 4, if not [i]messier[/i].[/b]

The pacing is genuinely... [i]puzzling[/i]. One second you're doing the hypest fight and setpiece of the last 3 games, and the next thing you know you're doing 4-5 hours of forced filler that barely advances the plot if at all.
The whole thing just drops off a cliff after the first chapter and spends the entire rest of the game STRUGGLING to climb back up.

Same thing goes for the gameplay.
We've [i]finally[/i] moved past the Y3 engine, so gone are the super stiff, jerky and janky controls that barely work. This is the engine that powers Zero. The controls are good.
But there's so much [i]garbage[/i] piled on top of the gameplay.
There's "extreme heat" mechanics that aren't that useful and half of the time just get in the way, and singlehandedly caused the addition of the "heat suppresion" button just to TRY to mitigate them.
There's a "wall slamming" mechanic that's super janky and cheap-looking and ALSO constantly gets in the way.
There's [b]weapon skill levelling[/b] that bars the use of certain weapons until you've grinded enough XP for that type of weapon with weaker variants of it.


There is... so much. SO MUCH. So much EVERYTHING.
The game constantly feels like it's crumbling under its own weight trying to add so much, and like 70% of it isn't that good, and the story and gameplay end up suffering for it.


...Not to mention how it harms [b]completion[/b]. I've been going for 100% on every game, successfully so far.
You wanna know what this game does?
[spoiler]You can't start NG+ off of premium adventure. Anything you do there is just lost if you try and do NG+, since you can only use your original clear file.
I had to stop, before the final boss, and do all the side content I was missing in one fell swoop, just to keep my levelling and completion rewards for the Legend difficulty run.

[b]Only for it to turn out that there's a BUG that locks out the final karaoke song if you pick a certain dialogue option halfway through the game with Haruka.
My 100% completion was barred by a random fucking thing that didn't seem like it would affect anything, because the developers didn't realize it would skip the trigger to unlock that.
The solution to this being to RESTART THE ENTIRE GAME ON NG+ AND PICK THE RIGHT OPTION THIS TIME, HAVING TO REDO ALL SUBSTORIES, HOSTESSES AND COLLECTIBLES BECAUSE THEY DON'T CARRY OVER.[/b][/spoiler]


It's... rough. It's a lot.
It's a game that's too big for its own good and where only like 30% of that whole is good and [b]should've[/b] been its own game without all the other stuff cluttering it and holding it back.



And yet...
As miserable as completing the game (and [i]dealing with that game-breaking bug[/i]) was, I can't bring myself in good faith to not recommend it.
It's objectively better than 3 and 4 in basically every way, and it's got some of the highest high points in the series.
It's just... MAN this is the most Yakuza game.

[H1]Introduction[/H1]
[I]Yakuza[/I] series’ writer, Masayoshi Yokoyama, once commented to 1UP.com that 2012’s [I]Yakuza 5[/I] would be like [I]Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas[/I] in terms of scope – it would be a huge game with expanded core concepts. [I]Y5[/I] – and by extension 2019’s [I]Yakuza 5 Remastered[/I] – notably ended up featuring 5 explorable locales, 5 playable characters, and 4 side stories on top of the already plentiful side content that games in the series are known for. It, in retrospect, was more ambitious than 2013’s [I]GTA V[/I] in some ways.

[H1]The New…[/H1]
[I]Y5R[/I] not only whisks us back to Kamurocho and Sotenbori, but also introduces us to Nagasugai (based on Nakasu, Fukuoka), Tsukimino (Susukino, Sapporo), and Kineicho (Sakae, Nagoya). It brings Kazuma Kiryu, Taiga Saejima and Shun Akiyama back as playable characters, with pop-idol-in-training Haruka Sawamura, and disgraced former baseball player Tatsuo Shinada being the surprising and welcomed additions to the roster.

If you’ve played the mainline remastered [I]Yakuza[/I] games so far, you’ll find [I]Y5R[/I]’s gameplay to be very familiar. There are ample substories to complete, minigames and gambling games to play, food and drinks to consume, hostesses to meet, fighting abilities to unlock, and trinkets to find. Not only do these side activities make locales more alive, they’re necessary for levelling up the protagonists for boss battles.

Yet, there is plenty that makes [I]Y5R[/I] different from its predecessors. The five playable protagonists each has at least one master to train with; extra training with Sotaro Komaki can raise the level cap from 20 to 25; health and abilities can be enhanced by dining in restaurants; Revelations are expanded to include some weapons; character- and region-specific minigames are added; and of course the 4 side stories.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3322945923
[H1]The Bad…[/H1]
All this new content is certainly impressive on paper, but sadly, bigger and more don’t translate to better. Although gameplay is diverse and abundant, the game is so bloated with content that the main story gets overshadowed and sidelined. Perhaps that was intentional because the main story was poorly thought out and is unnecessarily convoluted. More poignant themes and emotions were ignored in favour of forced storytelling and poor character developments, which Yokoyama tried to present as shocking narrative twists.

Just how bad is the main story? Prior to the final boss fight, Kiryu asked the antagonist, “What are you doing here?” (The actual reason for this is so ludicrous that I couldn’t blame Kiryu for asking.) Just when you thought the enemy’s motive is tied to the running theme of realizing one’s dream, and help other people fulfill theirs, he answered, “To be honest…I’m not really sure myself.” That was it – absolutely lazy writing to tie up a major loose end.

With 5 playable characters, pacing of the game dragged. Although Kiryu’s part kickstarted the story well, it stopped at a cliffhanger so that the game could shift to Saejima’s. However, Kiryu’s actions had no impact on Saejima’s adventures; Saejima’s exploits had no effect on Haruka and Akiyama’s experience; and Haruka and Akiyama’s deeds had no influence on Shinada’s circumstance. Each of the 4 parts exists in a vacuum, thus bringing the main story’s momentum vexingly to a halt 4 times, with no payoff for each until a huge exposition dump in the finale.

It was as though Yokoyama got tired of writing gangster stories, and was more interested in exploring other subject matter and telling smaller, more intimate stories in the [I]Yakuza[/I] universe. Thus, we got a slew of side activities and 4 side stories to distract us from the poor quality of the main narrative.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3322947560
[H1]The Saving Graces…[/H1]
Although the 4 side stories have little impact on Kiryu, Saejima, Haruka and Shinada (Akiyama doesn’t have one) in the main story (except for earning XPs), they’re memorable and touching. Kiryu getting caught in the world of street racing; Saejima confronting the harshness of nature in winter; Haruka balancing fame and friendship; and Shinada resolving old feuds with his rivals – they all have their moments that made me want to go the extra mile to finish tasks or missions. I actually cared about the characters involved.

Haruka and Shinada’s side stories and main story parts are particular standouts. Haruka’s section is full of positivity and hope, and allows for hassle-free exploration of Sotenbori. Shinada’s is full of pathos (and a laughable disguise from a masked individual), making you want to root for his comeback. Plus, Shinada is unrefined and rough around the edges in a funny way, but also feels real. I was really glad he was added as a playable character, even though his story is actually superfluous to the main narrative.

As bloated as [I]Y5R[/I] is, the gameplay is still fun overall. The most important part – the combat – is slick and tactical. While plenty of Heat Actions were at my disposal, I needed to learn to use them strategically for filling the Climax Heat gauge, which would allow me to use Climax Heat techniques during boss battles. With that, boss fights never felt very challenging at Normal difficulty level.

There was one detail that the developers included that I particularly loved. Because Shinada respects the game of baseball, he will not use a baseball as a weapon. If you try to pick up a dropped bat when controlling him during combat, you’ll see a unique animation of Shinada picking it up, inspecting it, then putting it down. It’s a small detail, but has great impact on characterization!

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3322947877
[H1]Final Thoughts[/H1]
Yokoyama also once said to 1UP.com about [I]Y5[/I], “Outside of whenever it’d be useful to preserve the tempo of the story scenes, we want to avoid cutting things off as much as we can.” Perhaps he and his fellow developers should have rethought that approach. Since more emphasis was put on the side content than the main story, valuing quantity over quality, [I]Y5R[/I] ended up being an uneven game. But, it’s still fun depending on the part you’re playing.

[I]Y5R[/I] is a product of the studio’s overambition, but it’s also proof of their collective creativity. After [I]Y5[/I], the studio went on to make [I]Yakuza 0[/I], which is arguably one of the best games (if not THE best game) in the series to date. [I]Y0[/I] – a game that also features multiple playable characters, concurrent storylines, and multitude of side content – feels more cohesive as a whole; it’s what [I]Y5[/I] could have been if the developers’ creativity was expressed with restraint.

As much as I’ve bagged on this game’s story, Yokoyama is not without talent. The game’s side stories were interesting; he also wrote a powerful scene in which Kiryu asked himself after seeing someone he holds dear got hurt, “Why does this happen whenever I get involved? Why does someone else always have to pay the price?” If only he went with this theme instead of spinning yarn about fulfilling dreams.

[I]Y5R[/I], in spite of its flaws, is still worth playing because there are plenty of good bits in the potpourri of content. If you plan on experiencing all that the [I]Yakuza[/I]/[I]Like a Dragon[/I] series has to offer, the good news is that [I]Y5R[/I] is far from being the worst game. Somewhere in this game, you’ll likely find some elements that will be of interest to you.

After the previous game, I can see how the RGG team decided to expand on the concept first experimented with in Y4. Yakuza 5 is a complete evolution of the gameplay and game structure first explored in the last entry. They went from four protagonists playing their stories in the same city, to having five different protagonists with an entire city for each of them (almost) to explore. This game is MASSIVE in all aspects that you can consider, which really surprised me when I first started playing it. 

Like the previous game, the story is split up into parts where each character takes front stage, with each restart putting you into a new city to explore, often filled with new activities to perform on as part of the many side contents you'll find around. On top of the main story which is connected to a bigger plot in between each of the character's segments, each protagonist also gets a side activity that gets briefly introduced as part of the main progression, that you can follow to take a break from the main gameplay loop and arguably play a completely different game on each. I do personally enjoyed these side modes a lot as I enjoy the great variety that this series offers on their side content.

As part of the main combat, it's pretty similar to the previous game's styles, besides the one character who is swapped for a new protagonist. One addition is a character specific way of spending their heat, which can be fun or annoying, depending on who you're using, Saejima's isn't that great and is more annoying than not when it triggers.

Completion wise, as expected from having five different cities, there is A LOT to do, as evident by my high play time logged, it is certainly a challenge for Completionists. Most of the actual objectives aren't all that difficult, there simply is an insane amount of things to do. One tip however: Play on Normal difficulty, Akiyama's Coliseum matches are NOT balanced for him and it is a pain to do them in Hard or higher. 
There's also the fact that for some god forsaken reason, they do not allow you to create Clear Save Files from Premium Adventure, and they explicitly tell you this. This means that if you plan to do future replays, you are only able to carry whatever progress you had at the Finale. I have no Idea why they chose to do this and I understand it's the only time they did, so... there's that.

Performance and engine wise, there is a massive improvement from Y4 Remastered, having played Y0, Kiwami and Kiwami 2, this game feels like a middle point between 0/K1 and K2, it is still the older engine but I really felt a big improvement that it almost feels like it's the Dragon Engine at times, transitions into battles are smooth and instant almost always, the other times they play a small cutscene to begin the fight, but that's mainly an aesthetic choice, though it can get annoying after repeated occurrences.

As a final comment, I often see people disliking this game a lot, and I feel like it mainly comes from it's massive length, I get it for a bit, but the game being built in five different stories and cities are what enable it to be this way. Another point may be that Haruka's sections are so different and pretty much it becomes a rhythm game altogether, as a fan of that genre myself I adored this part, but I could understand someone who may not be as ecstatic to be more annoyed by it than not, I do enjoy the big variety offered so I enjoyed this alternate play style when it came, it isn't as hard as I wish it could be at times, but mastering the harder opponents was a fun challenge.

Yakuza 5 takes on an ambitious scope, introducing four new cities and featuring five active main characters, each entwined in their own compelling subplot, all of which are individually impressive. However, the game grapples with the challenge of uniting these diverse elements, resulting in difficulty tying everything together. The main story, marked by a few notable highs, often falls short. A pivotal moment occurs when a main protagonist questions the purpose of their journey, encapsulating the sentiment that permeates Yakuza 5's main narrative. While the character subplots are exceptional in their own right, the cumulative effect feels a bit overwhelming.

Despite these challenges, Yakuza 5 boasts the most extensive collection of mini-games in the entire series. The combat system, unfortunately, remains largely unchanged from Yakuza 4. However, within Yakuza 5, one can discern the early DNA of Yakuza 0, with this game laying the foundation for the exceptional aspects later refined in Yakuza 0. Despite its shortcomings, Yakuza 5 retains the quintessential Yakuza charm, offering hilarious subplots, intense action, and a unique style synonymous with the series. On these merits alone, I recommend Yakuza 5 to devoted series fans looking to complete the entire saga. However, for others, it may be prudent to consider skipping this one.

While it did take me 106 hours to go through most of the content, I did enjoy the diversity and entirely new map, as well as bringing back most of the characters from Yakuza 4.

The graphics are a leap forward. This is I believe the first Yakuza that used the new engine where characters are more detailed and the environment looks better overall. I might be wrong, but I think this uses the same engine Kiwami and Yakuza 0 use. While graphics still look a bit dated, I would say it's an improvement comparing to 3 that looked like early PS3 game.

The story: The story is identical to Yakuza 4 where the entire game is split between different characters that all come up together in the end. I liked the story in Yakuza 4, and this one I felt added some more depth to it. Yeah there are still trope moments here and there, but at this point I kind of got used to it. Yakuza 0 had better story no doubt, but I would say I still enjoyed going through this story.

The gameplay: Now you have more things to do, especially how every character has a "sidestory" now. Sidestories are not to be confused with substories where it's just a side quest, sidestories are more like a special character quest where you get to experience different gameplay, for example early spoilers [spoiler] kiryu is now a taxi driver, so his sidestory involves driving a taxi car around the city [/spoiler]. This adds many hours of content, on top of new cities to explore and new things to do. Oh and no more stupid hostess club management game from Yakuza 3 and 4. Thank god, I really didn't like that game, I'd like to go back to management games from Kiwami 2 and 0. 
So on top of having ton of mini games, combat is improved. Enemy encounters are now marked with a red speech bubble, so unlike 3 and 4 where they hide in the corner and pounce on you, here you can actually recognize them from afar and avoid them if you don't want to engage in combat. However, there is still a problem where they react instantly in chasing you down, and some of them are even faster than you. Like I said in the previous games, the encounters are not a problem until the endgame where they become annoyance, and once again I can't stress how encounters are better done in 0, Kiwami and Kiwami 2. The combat itself is identical to 4, with addition to the "Climax heat" mode where characters get to do sort of a super move that does ton of damage. 
Speaking of gameplay, there is also a special character with a different gameplay. I won't spoil it, but I do have to say, I enjoyed it.

On top of all this, I am really glad how far Yakuza series have got. I really enjoyed playing this game and I only know Yakuza games get even better after this. Yakuza fans, do play this game, I really enjoyed my time with it, and I'll see you all in Ishin!

A good month and a half after my experiences with one of the highest points of the Yakuza series in [i]4[/i], and I was beyond excited to get back to the streets of Kamurocho... only to find myself on them for but a fraction of the game's runtime.

Indeed, [i]Yakuza 5[/i] is a veritable trot across Japan, as our five(!) protagonists find themselves all across the island nation and its cities. While Nagasugai, Tsukimino and Kineicho may not be as intricately designed as Kamurocho, I still really enjoyed my time exploring all of them – and returning to Sotenbori made for some of the game's best parts, though, of course, due in large part to the story and gameplay of its playable characters.

Let's talk about them, shall we? Kiryu, Saejima, and Akiyama all make a comeback, and Kir--, ehm, sorry, Taichi Suzuki definitely has the upper hand over the (other) two fourths of the legendary [i]Yakuza Four[/i]. While I love the taxi driving of Suzuki-san's part, let's just say that I'm a bit weary of running around prison courtyards as Saejima, and among the four sidestories, his was the only one I didn’t do everything in; on the other hand, Akiyama is totally robbed of having his own part of the game and an individual sidestory, even if I positively reveled in every moment he had to offer. Then we have Tatsuo Shinada, who totally surprised me with how much I ended up caring for him when all was said and done (don't tell me you didn't cry alongside him at the end), and taught me a helluva lot about baseball along the way.

Playing through parts one and two as Kiryu and Saejima respectively, things may start to seem a bit monotone by the end, but as part three begins my interest was immediately piqued when the words HARUKA SAWAMURA appeared on the screen. With her idol gameplay replacing dust-ups on the street with dance battles, the karaoke-on-steroids that is practicing and performing her three songs for the Princess League, and taking part in events and shows in the form of various minigames, that previously mentioned monotony is throughly broken into a thousand pieces. And that's not even mentioning her story, never mind [Part 3 spoiler][spoiler]her being reunited with Akiyama[/spoiler], I mean, [i]oh my god[/i]. Haruka-chan is the heart and soul of [i]Yakuza 5[/i], and I wouldn't have it any other way.

I'd always heard of [i]Yakuza 5[/i] being the longest game in the series, with many seemingly considering it too long, but nearing the end of the game I actively wished that there was even more to it. Especially as the story builds and builds and reaches a climax that just keeps on giving.

If [i]4[/i] was the highest point since [i]0[/i], then consider it beaten. [i]Yakuza 5[/i] aims incredibly high, and, honestly? It more than clears it.

You can tell playing it that the devs have kept a similar content structure with most of the series from Yakuza 5 to modern Yakuza/Like A Dragon games in 2025. This game has some pacing issues in gameplay chapters, the story can be overly complex & messy in areas, and different aspects of the game can be bloated, but there’s a whole lot to enjoy.

Yakuza 5 is best summed up as the individual stories being stronger than the ultimate endpoint. This is seen with the general storytelling and activities for each of the 5 characters. Each character feels unique due to a variety of factors like their specific minigame, their city, fighting style, etc.. Some substories, similar to Yakuza 4, are a bit specific per character as well (such as a substory focused on loans with Akiyama as this substory would be out of place if it was with any of the other 4 characters). Out of each character’s main story, some are much better told than others. Still, I enjoyed the overall storytelling for the most part as it’s generally a step-up from Yakuza 1-4. The combat and cutscene direction is also a clear step up from previous entries. Heat actions feel better, characters play similarly to previous games but with improvements, and leveling up is still fairly satisfying, if overly familiar. The boss fights, particularly in the finale, were fun with the QTE’s as well. The final boss? From a gameplay perspective, it might be my favorite in the series. The humor that the series is known for is in here as well although I think the sequel, Yakuza 0, is really when RGG knew how to consistently nail it. Lastly, it was a smart decision to break up the middle portion of the game by turning it into effectively a dancing game with catchy music as this helps break up the beat’em up gameplay. 

As for issues, it’s a bit of a double-edged sword with having 5 characters. The nature of having multiple characters with their own storyline and motivations can lead to a confusing story when there has to be a reason for all the protagonists to meet up in the end. One big issue in the storytelling is that sometimes, there are just too many twists for the sake of twists. This is made fully apparent in 2 sections of the game to me. There’s also pacing issues (some chapters really drag on) & some plot elements that make hardly any logical sense. The enemy encounter rates in this game are noticeably high so it’s kind’ve a pain to run around in the cities at times without a certain item equipped. Additionally, if you’re going for 100%, there’s a ton of content to get through, some of it superfluous and downright rage-inducing. Chicken Racing, Golf, Fishing, and Pool all come to mind as ‘bottom of the barrel’ minigames in the entire series and they’re all in this game, made much worse due to what you need to do in order to 100% the game. Lastly, the ending to Yakuza 4 is largely ignored and so it’s strange that 5, a direct sequel, took such a different direction with characters. Ultimately, it’s probably for the better decision as 5’s story, even with its faults, is much more engaging and captivating with what it does to returning characters. 

Criticisms aside, it’s great to play Yakuza 5 even a decade after it officially came out because it holds up. It really set the stage for not just it’s sequel, Yakuza 0, to shine but the series moving forward due to the captivating writing, interesting side characters, wide variety of side content, and wacky ideas. 8.5/10.

Edit: Added in extra details on how Yakuza 5 side content structure has largely been replicated for the rest of the series, which is a great thing since RGG has consistently shown starting with 5 and after, that they know how to make varied and fun side, large-scale minigames (i.e. the taxi side content in Yakuza 5 versus cabaret club side minigame in Yakuza 0) substories in addition to smaller minigames (darts, bowling, etc.).

Yakuza 5 is a bizarre entry into the franchise. On one hand there are tons of people who love it and on the other, tons who hate it. Was it the best it could’ve been, no, but it wasn’t the poorest either. It does clearly have big flaws, but I still absolutely enjoyed it. I thought the story was great too, with only a major issue with the ending plot twist and Saejima's part. I heard a good way to describe it is, it has some of the best but also worst parts in the franchise, which sums it up well. I would recommend digging deep into this game with the content you enjoy, and if you really want to, skip the content you don't. Almost every protagonist’s parts I loved, Saejima’s part being the only painful one. And it definitely did have those heartening and awesome moments the series is known for. The exploration was pretty cool, having five cities to explore. There were a few downsides to that though. For example, some of the new layouts were not the best for gameplay (Tsukimino) and their lighting and environment was just very poorly done. The gameplay was done well, maybe one of the most fun in terms of combat. And the side stories were a cool way to introduce an optional side plot to the game. Playing through all besides Saejima’a was amazing. Admittedly I did first dislike the batting minigame but soon grew into it.

[spoiler] At the beginning, that opening scene was a nice way to start. Showing how Kiryu and Haruka’s lives have changed. You can occasionally see how bad not being with his children is affecting him and a few substories add to that. The whole story between Haruka and Kiryu is always still so sentimental to me. I adore getting to see Haruka growing up and their love growing stronger with each game, it always makes me so sappy. Daigo still looks to Kiryu for assistance with leading the Tojo clan, even as Kiryu tries his hardest to leave his Yakuza past behind. I really enjoyed Tadashi and Mayumi, they were great characters. I honestly felt bad for Mayumi, wanting Kiryu as a partner. The whole ending battle was amazing, getting to fight hordes of Tojo members. The entire cutscene of Kiryu going against the Tojo was so badass. And his taxi side story and mini game was honestly really fun, especially the racing. The entire racing storyline was great, Nakajima’s whole past with his wife was so damn heartbreaking.

Saejima’s part was iffy at best, but man, was it really bad at worst. Unlike Y4, I found barely any enjoyment out of his section. The prison here was very slow and not enjoyable at all. Running back and forth, the boring “imagination” section, they were a real slog. The fact that he’s in prison again in the first place is just super exhausting. The snowmobile escape and the bear fight were the only things I enjoyed. Then into the city nothing was enjoyable or fun either. Saejima’s hunting side story was also very slow and boring. Saejima’s whole plot with kidnapping Kitakata was just not engaging. From someone who loves to be immersed and engaged with the stories in games, this has to be one of the most absurd for me. Which is actually really sad too, it no doubt could've been better than it was if they did it differently. He’s a good character, and it really showed in Y4 and in this finale, but his part was atrociously done and didn’t give him anything to go on.

Haruka & Akiyama’s part was also amazing. Having heard this part was very slow mainly from the mini games, but I actually loved doing them. That obviously doesn't mean everybody will, and I completely understand. Before playing, I originally thought it was going to drag on, but really around 90% of the mini games are optional anyway. Haruka’s story was a touching departure from the usual plot, though I know some may find it unappealing since it has nothing to do with the Yakuza plot and focuses on Haruka’s personal life until around the second half, but I always adore these heartening stories. It was adorable, and I feel showing Haruka’s POV was actually really nice to see, and I honestly loved her story more than I’d like to admit. Park being quite cold on the surface, was nice to see her eventually develop a sweet bond with Haruka. Then Park’s death caught me so off guard, especially after all that happened between them, and how brutal she died (no mercy for Ogita). It was great playing Akiyama again, an amazing character to see once more. Only to be reinforced when he meets with Haruka to solve Park’s murder together, that dialogue man. Akiyama is such an amazing wholesome guy, I’m really glad Akiyama and Haruka share a part. I know some would disagree, preferring that Akiyama had his own part, and don’t get me wrong, I’d love that too. But if it had to be anyone besides Kiryu, Akiyama was definitely a fantastic choice. I really wish he got a more balanced screen time though. Akiyama’s ending battle was short but amazing. I didn’t expect to find out that Majima was Park’s ex-husband. I do just wish Majima got more closure for Park in the finale, I felt that’s what was missing by the time I finished.

Shinada was also a fantastic additional character. Once a great baseball player, then permanently banned. 15 years later, starting with only 217 Yen to his name. I loved his part, nice development, nice pacing. His meteor tackle was pretty fun too. Moving through his story is quite calm at first, but soon picks up once Daigo comes to offer him the job of finding out what happened 15 years ago. Over the next few chapters you find yourself trying to put the pieces together one by one to figure out what’s going on. Soon chatting with Daigo which ends in a brawl. Daigo’s boss fight was really fun, maybe the most fun I’ve had fighting Daigo before. Battling along Sawada was unexpected but amazing. Overall, not much to say for Shinada’s part. That’s not a bad thing, it’s just a very straight forward part. A fantastic character with a fantastic well developed story, definitely an awesome addition.

Now the finale. The fighting itself was wildly fun throughout the entire section. [i]Only children believe in dragons.[/i] Oh, and Shinada jumpscare. I loved everyone’s opening sequences, the calm before the storm. We soon returned to Kiryu and Saejima to fight our way up Kamurocho Hills. Kiryu’s dialogue when Kurosawa walks away, ouch man. Then end up back as Haruka, loving her lead up to the Japan Dome. Then the four badasses fight hordes of enemies. Saejima meets with Majima and they fight. Shinada’s crying scene killed me. After a while, one would think that Kurosawa is the entire big bad of the game, rightly so, clearly built up to him from the start of the game. WRONG. It's Aizawa, surprise. The finale was built up to be so good too. The boys come together, Haruka is singing her heart out, and everything is set up perfectly. Then Aizawa, no build up, literally only seeing him a few times in the entire story. His entire character is just him wanting to surpass Kiryu, not even caring that his father wanted to give him everything. Funny enough, Ryuji in Y2 had a similar goal. The major difference, Ryuji actually had a fantastic build up and well developed character arc. However, the actual boss fight at Tojo HQ, although tough, was awesome to do. Moving on to the rest of the ending. I did not expect it to hit me that hard, but it did. Haruka giving her speech was such a fantastic scene. I still ended up loving the finale, ignoring Aizawa. To end this off, I'd like to talk about the taxi minigame. In my honest opinion, it's the worst minigame in all of Yakuza. Never in my life have I seen such horrible artificial intelligence. There's a penalty called 'Contact' that triggers when your taxi touches something. That wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for pedestrians to be so awfully coded that even when you're already driving over a crosswalk, they'll still attempt to cross the road. And, because pedestrians touching the side of your vehicle is also contact, you'll receive a penalty and are reset to the last checkpoint. Keep in mind, in this minigame, you'll have to reach your destination on a timer, so a reset can cost an incredibly frustrating amount of your precious time.

Playing through the entire Yakuza franchise, and 5 is a new low. I can appreciate the ambition and scope of the game, but it very clearly collapsed under its own weight. Narrative-wise, it is easily the messiest game in the series, somehow surpassing 4's laughably awful story with its exposition, conveniences, and surprise reveals. 

The Kiryu section was entertaining enough that I was hopeful that it would be a better experience overall than 4. Kiryu is still very fun to play and has by far the most options during combat. The story for his chapter was also decently intriguing and was set up pretty well. 

Saejima's section is where it all goes to shit. His gameplay is fun enough, when those charge attack hits land they are incredibly satisfying, but his section is an absolute snoozefest to get through, and I genuinely can't believe people thought it was a good idea to add in a hunting section in the game. Starting from the prison section which goes on far too long, to being forced to play through an imaginary Sapporo, to the mentioned hunting village, it legitimately made me drop the game for a month before I finished it again because it was so exhausting and mindnumbingly boring. 

Akiyama and Haruka's section is incredibly mixed. I actually found myself enjoying Haruka's section and gameplay. The story is no Perfect Blue but it still does a pretty good job making me feel repulsed towards Japan's idol industry. I can definitely see why people would hate it though, I'm sure it's jarring to go from a beat em up game to a rhythm game for the next 5 or so hours. Akiyama's story I don't remember at all, and his gameplay is atrocious. He does pitiful damage, has almost no defensive options, and in general feels incredibly scuffed compared to 4. His final fight where Kanai gangs up on you is just miserable to play through, almost as bad as Tanimura's fight against Munakata in 4. I get that I'm playing Hard mode but I don't see how being knocked around like a pinball by Kanai and his goons are supposed to help me get better at the game. 

Shinada has an interesting story but the way its connected to everyone else is nonsensical and felt like the developers pulled it out of their ass. His gameplay is also incredibly unfun, and using weapons doesn't make it any better. 

The final chapter is just exposition, exposition, exposition. At that point, I genuinely couldn't care less about what was going on, because it was just convenience and contrivances one after another with exposition, exposition, and exposition. Has it sunk in yet? This game in general has the most egregious usage of unskippable cutscenes and dialogue in any of the Yakuza games to date. My E key is probably broken from skipping all the worthless padding and filler for so long. I feel like the story would've been nonsensical even if I didn't start skipping everything, the plans that the characters come up with are so incredibly dumb, like that mastermind reveal ploy where they all fight each other. 

Maybe it's recency bias, but this game is easily the worst in the series, because while 4's story was awful and ruined Saejima's character as a whole with rubber bullets, at least it wasn't this long or this much of a slog (although it was because 4's continuous backstabs from characters reached comedic levels). The only new character I remember from this game is Shigeki Baba, who is admittedly handled well because I found him compelling with his split loyalty. Every other new character I've forgotten already. 

As a whole, I'm just done with the multiple protagonist route with Yakuza and can't wait to just play Kiryu the entire game in 6.

Don't get me wrong, I absolutely love this series, I'm hooked and I can't wait to see how the story progresses, but Yakuza 5 with 5 playable main characters makes it a little too complicated and unbearably long. Also I think the [spoiler] "Oh no, they died! Or did they?" and "Oh no they are evil! Or are they?" [/spoiler] revelations are getting a little too overused. I felt like this game in particular was way too saturated with them, making the plot extremely predictable. 

I also found it rather frustrating how long it takes to get to the main story, and having five main character's stories at the same time makes it hard to keep up with what's happening. Having a lot of characters gives the game a lot of diversity and an insane amount of content sure, but it can be difficult to keep the story easy to follow.

[code]Yakuza 5 offers more content than any other game in the franchise up to that point – but what could’ve been its biggest strength is unfortunately also its biggest weakness. Significant pacing issues and head-scratching story moments occasionally make this game a slog to play through[/code]

Five character to play as, five cities to explore & all the gameplay that fans of the franchise expect: [i]Yakuza 5[/i] doesn’t want to innovate, [i]Yakuza 5[/i] wants to expand. As such, there's more of everything - even if that everything is mostly what we've seen in previous [i]Yakuza[/i] games already. Just reaching the end of [i]Yakuza 5[/i]'s story, ignoring all side content, is going to take even experienced (!) players between 30 and 35 hours. If you fancy taking a look at some of the side content as well, you can easily put a few dozen hours on top of that: [i]Yakuza 5[/i] is simply bursting with activities to participate in.

Unfortunately, more doesn't always mean better. That is, unless you're only mostly interested in side-activities to begin with - if you just want to participate in karaoke with different playable characters, well, there you go.

No, the main victim of [i]Yakuza 5[/i]'s content expansion is the main story. Just like [i]Yakuza 4[/i], it's spread across different playable characters, each with their own parts & chapters - culminating in a finale where everything's supposed to come together. While its predecessor featured four playable characters, [i]Yakuza 5[/i] ramped that number up to five. How does that work out?

Unfortunately, for everyone expecting an interwoven storyline with frequent crossovers between the (playable) characters, I'm going to have some disappointing news: [i]Yakuza 5[/i] has chosen a different approach, a sequential one. To put it simply, you're playing through the story of the first protagonist, get a cliffhanger to set up that finale and then start from zero with another protagonist in an entire different city/setting. Rinse and repeat until the finale has been reached.

Considering you're not allowed to transfer anything - be it items or money - between characters up until that finale, [i]Yakuza 5[/i] feels more like a package deal for a bunch of separate games rather than one big title with a steadily progressing story. It's more of an episodic title with a big crossover at the end, if you will.

There are three problems with the approach [i]Yakuza 5[/i] is taking: the need for good pacing, delivering satisfying end points for each individual story part and lastly, offering a finale that manages to tie all loose threads together. And as you guessed it, [i]Yakuza 5[/i] has problems with all of these.

Let’s start with the pacing issues. What’s the most important part about a story which is supposed to come together at the big finale? Getting the players to stay interested until the awaited conclusion arrives with a bang. In an episodic title, this means giving the players a constant stream of plot development or clues throughout all episodes, without running out of steam in-between. That is unfortunately nothing [i]Yakuza 5[/i] can provide.

In a game as filled with potential side activities, it’s easy for the player to stray too far from the story, creating their own pacing problems by spending too much time perfecting those karaoke numbers for example. But [i]Yakuza 5[/i] manages to create its own pacing problems even when ignoring side activities. The pacing of the game changes constantly. Sometimes it’s pressing on rapidly, queuing long cutscenes and dialogues without breaks. Sometimes it stalls you, forces you to run through a city multiple times before the story really continues.

This isn’t a new issue for the franchise - but it gets worse thanks to the game’s length, constant progress resetting by switching to new characters and the unsatisfying end points of the story arcs, which brings us to problem number 2: None of the character parts have a satisfying end. Instead, the endings all point directly to the finale, leaving you with just a feeling that the “princess is in another castle”. Nothing really gets resolved during each part, [i]Yakuza 5[/i] just dumps a lot of loose threads on you with the promise to tie them up in the end. Completing an episode, which – again – takes a few hours, doesn’t give you the feeling of completing an interim goal – it feels like someone just pulled that dangling carrot in front of you a little further away.

And then, lastly, we get to the promised, solve-it-all part: the finale of the game. Of course, due to spoilers, I won’t go into details here, just let me say this much: First, you’re going to see a lot of dialogues painstakingly trying to tie everything together. Second, you’ll realize that thanks to the length and uneven pacing of this game, you’ve already forgotten some of the earlier plot details. Third, even with all the time to build things up, [i]Yakuza 5[/i] still decides to throw some last-minute surprise developments into the mix. Lastly, while some of the character moments still work due to the attachment we’ve gotten to them over the last few games, others are just bafflingly stupid.

That’s not something that just happens during the finale, by the way. Of course, being a [i]Yakuza[/i] game, a bit of stupidity is expected – like the inconsistent use and power of guns in these games. However, [i]Yakuza 5[/i] takes things up a notch at times, which made me really wonder if some of the characters are just plain idiots. And this is a franchise where you fight a tiger with your plain fists as a boss battle.

Overall, the story of [i]Yakuza 5[/i] made me tired, scratch my head and even consider dropping the game a few times. Still, I do have to give the game some credit where it’s due: the voice acting remains fantastic, and I can’t help but love some of the characters. Returning to Kamurocho, with Kiryu standing under that big neon arc, is always a pleasure. Punching gangsters with a bike feels great (even though this game has way too many random encounters in narrow streets & blocking enemies). I enjoyed the gameplay change introduced with the third playable character, even if they overdid it. And well, there’s always baka mitai.

Still, [i]Yakuza 5[/i] is probably my least favorite Yakuza game I played so far. It didn’t stop me from trying to get all the way to [i]Yakuza 6[/i] but it sure did test my patience a few times. If you’re like me, you’re probably going to play this game regardless, just to continue Kiryu’s journey. But if it wasn’t for this and the attachment I developed for the franchise, I doubt I could’ve seen this game to its end. Replaying it is certainly out of the question.

Honestly, Yakuza 5 just doesn't cut it as a good Yakuza game. I tried it out because I had played 0 first, and this game inspired 0, so I expected much more from it, but this game feels so drag-on, tutorial-filled, and non-action-packed. I just thought this game was too packed with side stuff. This is usually where Yakuza games shine for most people but it can get repetitive and boring fast doing the same thing over and over again, and especially you'll have to do these things 5 times each because each character has something new for them to do. There also is no CP or unlockable abilities like earlier games so everything has to be done by constant trips and while walking, bottomless stomach, sprinting, or anything. This means that for each new character you play as there will be the same "Learn from Masters, Do Side Story, See all Revelations, Visit all Restaurants, Do Touring, Increase Weapon Skill, Play Minigames, Fight In Victory Road, Complete Hostess, repeat." for each character all while being hounded by the numerous fighting encounters that they can drag you into, as well as the countless backtracking and trips you'll have to do. The Level Ups also are so strange and disorganized. The fights also give out pretty cheap rewards, and also And the story? Ok but a bit underperforming in my opinion. Every time you get into the city there's always many things hounding you from progression, such as a substory or a revelation, or a certain enemy that sneaks up on you causing needless encounters, and there are far too many of these. And, even when it LOOKS like something interesting will happen, there are needless dialogue scenes between story events to make the game feel longer than it actually should be. There are returning ones like Yuya, Majima, Kamiyama, and Komaki, but everyone just feels so "meh". Completely disagree with other opinions regarding this as a masterpiece, or even one of the strongest entries in the Yakuza series.  This is one of the most [i]different[/i] in the Yakuza series, which doesn't necessarily translate to good.  

The problem is, the game is trying to do too much, and be too much at the same time.  This contributes to a lack of focus, poor storytelling, and pacing. 

There are multiple characters to play as this time, and each character has a story, alongside their 'regular activity' simulator.  Kiryu has his story in the first chapter, and along with it, you also drive a taxi.  A lot.  Saejima goes hunting.  But the worst... the worst is Haruka.  There's an entire seemingly interminable chapter dedicated to her.  It's a cliched, trope-filled 'story' as she chases a dream to become an idol because reasons. Instead of fighting, there are dancing minigames in which we have to match button presses as they appear on screen, while she performs passionless robotic movements with dull lifeless eyes gazing out in innocent wonder at the world.   I lost all interest in the game at this point and only continued as I had heard that Yakuza 6 was a direct continuation of this story.

Speaking of which, the stories of each character is supposed to be interwoven, but they decided to go with a cliffhanger at the end of each character's chapter, which results in a rushed, dissonant final chapter.  It doesn't help either that the plot is very convoluted with a lot of references to other people and their machinations, and I am not convinced the writers themselves know what is going on. Several times, they had to rely on expositions and even then it took a long time to get through it.  

The fighting itself, which is the main attraction of these games, is decent in its combos and heat moves.  Each character has their own best moves and combos, but due to the massive gaps in playing between them, I found I was forgetting a lot of what made them strong.  Despite that, I found that the boss fights weren't very action packed or satisfactory, they were just OK and most were quite simple, and over very quickly.

An interesting mechanic that's unlocked this time is the second health bar, filled only by food but not restorable through medicine.  It makes for a nice advantage before you're about to head into a big fight.  

The towns are, as usual, nice to explore; there's a decent amount of detail and places to shop and eat.  But, due to the multiple locations, eventually the exploration became a wearisome task.  


I do hope Yakuza 6 isn't more of this.

It pains me, but Yakuza 5 is probably my least favorite game in the series that I've played so far. I genuinely disliked the game for the vast majority of its runtime.

The game just does a repeated thing where it kneecaps itself every time anything gets good. A new mechanic is introduced, and either you're bogged down in tutorials for ages, or the game gets weirdly hard and gatekeeps progress on some terrible mini game. The characters draw you in but then keep acting out of character so the story can hit the same beats that Yakuza 1-4 did. The flow of the game starts to find its footing, and then it misses hard on too many boring cutscenes or exposition or random errands that waste your time.

But where the pain really hits is in the story. Every time the game sets up an interesting thread, it drops it to move onto something new. It's almost like they don't trust their audience to follow a story lead for more than a few hours at a time, but then they expect them to remember everything by the end? Honestly this game just didn't interest me enough and I dropped it for months at a time, which is the first time that's happened for a Yakuza game for me. I deeply care about all of these characters (even the new baseball guy isn't that bad) but the game just wrongfoots itself so often I was often wondering what the writers were thinking. Did you really have to mangle a character motivation so bad, just to set up a contrived boss encounter nobody needed? Again and again and again??

Unfortunately the combat just had not matured enough in the series lineup for Y5 either. Many of the bosses follow the game pattern as in Y3 and Y4 - a lot of cheap blocking and undodgable moves. Even on the Easy difficulty I found myself screaming at the screen when the boss whittles my health down on a series of moves I can't dodge while they block every attack I have. This is compounded by constantly switching characters so you never feel like you have solid grounding to learn and remember how to play each character well. The combat can flow ok bit I found myself deeply annoyed by most of the combat, which is in contrast to how much I enjoyed and would get into fights on purpose in Y0 and the Kiwamis.

So here I am, with a bunch of characters I love, but in a game where the focus changes so fast I can't stay interested, with a combat system still too full of legacy jank. There are good things for sure (Haruka's content is the best in the game by far) and there are some good meaningful moments between characters, but they come between many hours of straight up stupid character motives, predictable "oh they're doing that plot again" pivots that kneecap the tension or mystery, plodding combat, and just terrible awful boss encounters.

You can see where the team was starting to expand their palate. The scope is large, and the story takes over 30 hours to beat. A lot of side content too. Yakuza 0 owes a lot to this game. But also, Yakuza 0 is a masterpiece, and Yakuza 5 is extremely, intensely flawed.

[b]The best & biggest of the three "Remasters".[/b]

Compared to the original Yakuza 5, the only changes made are with the translations, as well as a few very minor dialogue bits not even being subtitled at all for whatever reason. The pachinko minigame is still missing here like in Yakuza 4 Remastered due to potentially dumb reasons.

The game takes place a couple of years after the fourth game, and unlike the previous game, you start  off with Kiryu this time, only he's a taxi driver in a completely different town. Also like the last game, it features multiple characters each with their own stories, except for two of them who share a whole chapter. All the characters aside from one are familiar faces if you've played the previous game. There's Kiryu, Saejima, Haruka, Akiyama, and the new character, Shinada.
Once again, the characters' stories get really intriguing until big reveals & twists start happening near the end of the game, making a lot of emotional & dramatic story bits in earlier chapters seem pointless. All of a sudden some characters aren't who they say they are and they're actually connected to these people, their true motivations are actually this & that so you're just supposed to forget some of that exposition you heard before, and so on; it gets kind of annoying to follow along with how much of that there is, but it's not as crazy as the last game.

Just like with the previous "remasters", they did some "re-translating" for this game as well. Here though, it feels like it's the most obnoxious "re-translation" work so far, namely during the text-based cutscenes. Never mind not actually translating what the dialogue said, but so many times during these cutscenes, the text is way too long or way too short compared to what was just said, so you end up reading too fast or too slow before the next line comes. Other times, they add things like "haha" or "..." in the middle of sentences when you can clearly hear that the dialogue itself never even had those. It's really like they're re-writing the script or something.

The combat here's a bit improved from the last game overall. 
A lot of Heat Actions are a lot more lenient in their trigger requirements now. Enemies have far fewer animations where they're invulnerable so you're more free to attack and grab them without missing when something looked like it should have connected.
The three familiar characters play almost exactly the same as the previous game. Haruka's the most notable for being the only one who doesn't actually do any fighting in the game, but rather her gameplay being solely focused on minigames and substories. The new character, Shinada, may take some getting used to, at least on the harder difficulties where enemies dodge & block more often as Shinada's attacks are really slow and often not big enough to connect to enemies. His extremely improvised-looking fighting style is at least interesting once you upgrade his stuff and learn how to properly use his moves.

Compared to the previous "remasters", this is also the most optimized game of the three, at least with the fan-patch. In the previous games, the fan-patches barely did anything, whereas here I've only ever crashed once during my whole time with the game, and I've never had any frame skipping issues either.

If you got into the previous game, you'll most likely get into this game as well.

Yakuza 4 was funny, with all the twists being as ridiculous as they were. Even though it had some pacing problems and tedious minigames, it still felt more compelling and motivating to play through than 5. 
Yakuza 5 feels like they completely forgot the epiphanies they made characters declare in 4. the ending also makes no sense and makes everything feel completely pointless.
There's no way to go through this other than every single chapter. 
I am going to spoil the entire game in this review.

Beginning with Kiryu's chapter, did anyone else feel excited when Kiryu left off four saying, "I'm the one who forced the tojo clan on you. Left you on your own. But now.. Im done running. Its time I take responsibility for my mistakes." only for his chapter to start... And he is a FUCKING TAXI DRIVER., in another city, pretending not to know Daigo or the Tojo clan?

It made me go wtf is he doing? and I was hoping they could explain this in a way that makes sense. But it doesn't because the game doesn't tie up loose ends from yakuza 4. I mean, holy shit, we see Kiryu with the Tojo at the end of 4, swearing in the saejima family and all; he jumped ship that fast?

This is all a part of Kiryu's internal conflict of not wanting to be involved with the yakuza because of his family. Yet, he involves himself in yakuza problems because he likes beating people up. I know everything Kiryu does in 5 is connected to how he can escape his fate as a yakuza, but Kiryu doesn't get close to solving this in this game.
In fact, at the end of the game, Kiryu ends up in the same situation as y1, 2, and 3. fighting some guy that wants to take over the tojo clan or something.

I started having a problem with Kiryu just because of this. He uses Daigo and everyone else in the tojo as cover for him until they can't cover for him anymore. He did that in the past games, but the nice part about 4 was him saying he'd stop doing that.
Well, he didn't stop doing that, and now he will go superhero mode again to fix everything.

Kiryu ACTS like he is some wise genius, but he doesn't think about his actions. He never takes responsibility. He only runs until he literally can't anymore. 
I wouldve been OK with this if they addressed how selfish Kiryu is and how he contradicted himself, but we get......
nothing
I would've liked the game 10x more if they developed Kiryu, but they make him go tojo superhero again. 
They also don't explain why Kiryu flipped the switch from his epiphany in yakuza 4. I get that it might've been because of Haruka pursuing being an idol, but I feel like it's different than that.
It just sucks when they build Kiryu up to be something to admire. Yeah, his physical strength is crazy but everything else? He is a disaster.

Very long Kiryu rant, but saejimas part is decent. It gets very dull in the last half, but his being in prison again is better than it was in 4. the nice part about his prison sequence is the people he meets; they are pretty interesting characters. Baba wasn't that bad either; they made a two-sided character that was good for once.
It is funny that saejima wants to make everyone his sworn brother. His parts made me appreciate him more as a character; even the showdown between him and majima were good. How he consoles other characters honestly to God makes him better than Kiryu. He is a genuinely good guy who doesn't fake his wisdom like Kiryu.

The fanbase of yakuza only cares about brawling mechanics, even though it steadily worsens from 3-5. Haruka's part of the story was a great breath of air. If I didn't have it, I would've suffered. They built up Haruka's character in this one, and it was great seeing her independent from Kiryu. It was also sweet seeing Haruka bond with the park. 

Park is one of the only exciting women characters in the series so far, as she is so ambitious. Seeing her try and be a mother figure for Haruka was great, and I liked that.
It started great, so that they couldn't have ruined it. Surprisingly they did! 
Park ends up telling her sob story, but it's a pretty good one. It made me respect her a lot more, except she introduces the central theme of yakuza 5... which is following your dreams.
She failed and couldn't follow her dream anymore, so she wants Haruka to pursue her dream. This wasn't a problem, but she got murdered for what we find out later, no reason. 
It's revealed that her ex-husband was majima, and majima wrote her a letter telling her he wanted to see her again??? 

So she was murdered for the letter, but they couldn't find it, and then they chased Haruka for it. They never get the letter, and it turns out that katsuya was best friends with park and didn't want her to die anyway.
While her death was an accident because of ogita, the entire majima letter plotline was stupid.. as the Osaka enterprise family and Kurosawa family go from desperately trying to get the letter to literally never mentioning or caring about it ever again by the end of Haruka's story. 

Then we have yet to receive confirmation from majima that he even wrote the letter, or why he wrote that letter... or anything. We get speculation from Akiyama and no epilogue resolving this part of the story. WHICH IS INSANE. YOUR TELLING ME MAJIMA DATED PARK WHEN SHE WAS LIKE 18 AN HE WAS IN HIS 30S, KNOCKED HER UP THEN SLAPPED HER WHEN SHE GOT AN ABORTION????? AN WE GET NOTHING MORE???

I liked Akiyama's part in the story, but he served to get Haruka's part over with. 
What was ridiculous was how everyone gave everything to ensure Haruka finished the park's dream of the japan dome; even Haruka wanted to do it! She was super stubborn and didn't want NOT to do it. But as soon as she saw Kiryu fighting on tv after the first song they performed, she instantly gave all of that up. 

Like, are you fucking kidding me???????? This just proved Park's point that Kiryu doesn't seem to let his kids be independent; they all rely on him. they genuinely do. Park was never cruel. She was telling the truth. While it's messed up for park to have projected herself so much on Haruka, she indisputably gave her lots of care and opportunity. 
But anyway, she gives up after everyone fights to keep Haruka on stage. So much for the main message being "pass your dreams onto others."

Then Haruka is running over the Kiryu as he's bleeding out... for the 3rd or 4th time in the series. That was incredibly disappointing to see. Especially when Haruka gave her speech, it was heartwarming until she said, "I can't keep singing!" like, are you for real? 
She had just left her role as the caretaker of the kiryus orphanage and the caretaker of Kiryu himself. Her character development seemed to be for nothing, all of everyone's sacrifices, for nothing. 

They could've had someone else rescue Kiryu instead of Haruka. If they had done that, it would've saved the entire ending. 

Overall the story had a lot of potential, but it didn't hit the mark. I would've been satisfied if they had made an epilogue that wrapped up some loose points.

Yakuza 5 is more or less the same deal as most of the other mainline Yakuza games, however it has its' own kinda unique ups and downs. 
So first the good stuff: 1) Combat is solid and responsive (minus the forever garbage lock on system of the series), there are 5 characters you can play as and 4 of them have extremely distinct fighting styles out of which 3 are good and 1 is pretty meh (1 of the characters doesn't really have fights per se). 2) You get to explore 5 cities which is unheard of in this series and I loved that, all of the cities have their own unique flair and style. And on top of that you also visit couple of other smaller locales (like a mountain hunting ground, a prison etc.) 3) There is lots and lots of extra content, like substories, side missions and activities, crafting, mini-games, dating sim (kinda), arena fights and other things like that. 4) Music in this game is awesome. There are a number of different styles/genres of music included and I enjoyed most of it, especially combat themes for the characters and the climactic battles. 5) I haven't played Y3 and Y4 so Akiyama was a new character for me and I gotta say I loved him and his super slick and fun fighting style.
As for the bad stuff: 1) This was the easiest Yakuza I have played yet. The only challenging part of this game was the Amon fights where I died 3 times (I died 4 times total in this game on hard difficulty). And btw the Amon fights, even though were not THAT hard, they were EXTREMELY annoying and awfully crafted, especially Kiryu's and Tatsuo's fights. While on the other hand, the other two were very easy (especially Saejima's fight). 2) Even though there are a lot of side activities to get into, almost all of them are very dull or they become very dull in a short while because most of these side activities tend to be way longer than they have the right to be. And that is basically the whole "thing" with Yakuza 5. 3) The upgrading system is very streamlined and easy to understand, however they decided to block your progress at lvl 20 until you get to the endgame and that part annoyed the living s..t out of me because all the exp you gain after 20 is lost until you get to the end. 4) Kiryu and Saejima are so strong that they completely overshadow the other 2 fighting characters when you have a choice to make. Those two are broken especially Saejima, because he has an ability where his attacks cannot be interrupted in heat mode and as you keep attacking you gain a lot of heat so you are always in heat mode and the dude is completely impossible to stop so that throws out any kind of challenge this game can provide while on the other hand, Kiryu's tiger drop deals so much damage that it is just at cosmic levels of insane. 5) The story starts out being very interesting, however during the second half of the game you will experience constant IQ level drops as the story gets dumber and dumber as if you are falling down a bottomless pit of stupidity and I am not talking about that "over the top anime funny" type of stupidity. 6) Even though this game is not the longest Yakuza game I have played, it really felt like it because it got so boring and needlessly drawn out that I struggled to get to the end. After I finished up the 4th character and I thought I was at the end, the game introduced a fifth character with his own story, side-missions and everything and I wanted to smash my head against my monitor repeatedly because I was already bored to death by the second half of the 3rd character (which is the non-fighting one) and on top of that I hated the 5th guy which was completely based on baseball that I hate (sorry baseball fans :D ). And his fighting style involves a lot around weapons and I hate using weapons in Yakuza so yeah not a happy-fun time for me. 7) This game felt hella wonky and would have definitely benefited from a Kiwami remake in my opinion so I kinda regret playing it in this format.
In conclusion, the cons largely outweighed the pros for me with this one, however I still think that Yakuza 5 is better than Kiwami 1 in almost every way but the main problem with Yakuza 5 said in one sentence is: It severely overstays its' welcome. 
And now I really don't want to play the other remasters (3 ,4) in hopes that they might someday release kiwami versions of them and possibly make them better. So I would only recommend this game for relatively die-hard Yakuza fans who want to experience all of what this series has to offer, otherwise just skip this one.
