The problem with Yakuza 5 is the failure of it's penta-narrative. Y4 used a quad-narrative that worked, but only because each character was either directly impacted or entangled in the main narrative elements. Y5 fails because each character is basically doing their own thing unrelated to everyone else, until the last 15 or so minutes of their parts.

	The biggest perpetrators of this are Haruka and Shinada's parts. Saejima is related to the larger plot, but spends a lot of time on irrelevant material. Kiryu's is the only strong chapter that directly builds up the main plotline. Let's delve into that first.

	Kiryu is currently supporting his orphanage financially via taxi driving. Haruka was scouted by a talent agency, and without giving too much away let's just say that Kiryu leaves so that she can follow her ambitions untethered. Kiryu picks up a passenger early on: Dojima, the current chairman of the Tojo clan. We get the setup right away: the current Omi chairman is gravely ill and will pass soon, so the current alliance between them and the Tojo is under threat of dissolution. Dojima is therefore seeking alliances elsewhere. He goes missing soon after.

	Kiryu, as was the case with the other games, doesn't want any part in underworld events. But he's slowly drawn into the fray, and with a resolution and drive that was missing in Y4 (which made his inclusion feel shoe-horned). Kiryu accepts his legendary status and reasons that it can be a force for good to protect those in his life. If the game stayed on Kiryu it would've had a stronger narrative.

	But then we get the narrative switching. Seajima is the first up, and at first it isn't too bad. He's (willingly) serving a 2 year prison sentence, but abruptly denied parole for no apparent reason. Without spoiling a lot, let's just say that an urgent matter comes up with Majima, so we bust out of prison. Once out we patrol Tsukimino (the local city) in search of the local clan leader, who is [i]allegedly[/i] behind the transgressions.

	The problem is that a large chunk of the chapter takes place in this tiny prison yard where you talk to the same 3 people to progress the story. And most of the story deals with Saejma's prison pals and the warden's ethics. It's not that interesting, or related to the larger narrative. When we finally get to a new city, the game rushes towards the end for the character switch.

	Next up is Haruka, who is working at an idol agency and gearing up for a local competition. Where's Daigo? What's happening with Majima? Who cares; you have a handshake event today! I hope you enjoy playing Idolmaster for the following 30 hours! Haruka's part has a character switch to Akiyama halfway in, which ties it back to the main story via an Omi Alliance run talent agency. But this part also sucks because they NERFED THE HELL out of Akiyama's moveset. He's real weak.

	Character switch to Shinada - an ex professional baseball player kicked out of the league for suspected match fixing. He lives life as an impoverished sleaze magazine writer. He begins uncovering the truth of his past as he seeks out the mysterious Nagoya family, whom are allegedly behind his downfall. His motivation being, at first, money from a 'mystery' benefactor (in a bad disguise). The mystery deepens as Shinada finds that the Nagoya family is seemingly nowhere (and everywhere) to be found.

	I think by now the issue I talked about at the start is more clearly laid out now. Completely unrelated storylines that detract from the main narrative. There is a silver lining, which is that Haruka's part is at least conceptually interesting. You dance instead of fight. And Shinada's is a good mystery. But it's completely out of place in the game. Akin to filler material that barely moves the story. Remember, this is about Daigo and the Tojo alliance, so when we connect Haruka and Shinada to the main story it's both silly, confusing, and still inconsequential

	By the ending, Kiryu is the only one with any real motivation for being there. Saejima is there as a Tojo soldier. Fine. Shinada is just helping out, I guess. Akiyama is there to take care of Haruka. And Haruka is dancing in the background at a concert. Which is under jeopardy for no discernible reason other than she is a main character and has to be in the finale. 

	The writing is all over the place. It works for the most part. But you frequently have characters fighting for no reason. Like Shinada's fight in the finale. Shinada is attempting to stop a shooting, but the shooter decides to not go through with it before Shinada arrives. Shinada still fights him because we need a boss fight for Shinada.

	Similarly, Saejima's part has him making up and shaking hands with an ally, only to fight him anyway because...I don't know, actually. There's no reason to fight someone after you've made up. We needed a boss fight to close up the chapter. Speaking of, after the fight Saejima is asked if he wants to know who the mastermind is behind everything and he passes because 'it won't change anything'. Just, really, the best writers behind this product! 

	Oh, and let's not forget this 4-way boss battle towards the end between allies: “we have to draw out the mastermind by killing each other. Whoever survives can end this”. That's not an exaggeration by the way, allies helping each other bring up the possibility of murdering each other in the off chance that the mastermind might decide to show himself (and reveal his nonsensical plot of shooting a girl at a concert? Lol WHY?). Really, really, really smart and realistic writing here. Award winning brilliance.
	
Don't think about the plot too much, because then it falls apart. The entire Majima story really went nowhere and was rather pointless. Sanada went to Tokyo because of his old coach, but we never meet him or resolve that matter. 

	This game was hard to get through. Everywhere else it's typical Yakuza: boring hostess convos, the mini games, pool, darts, etc etc etc. You know what to expect. Each character has a unique side-game that is interesting, but nothing you can make a full game out of. Everything else is fine. But, this being a story heavy franchise, it fails tremendously at that. Certain plot elements (Majima's story, Shinada going to Tokyo to meet his old coach) either don't get resolved or go nowhere when you think about it. So give the writing as much introspection as the writers did: barely any. 

	I'd suggest running through this quick and putting it behind you. Y4 may have been silly in it's plot elements, but Y5 is just trash.

I don't like this game. It's hard to tell whether RGG Studio was running out of ideas or had too many. Things I don't like about it:

- The story is split between five characters and the narrative suffers for it in the same way 4 did, i.e. it has a stop-and-start cadence where every time the plot picks up and gets interesting their part suddenly ends and you start from zero with a different character. I thought this would be less of a problem in 5 since most of the characters had already been established in the series, but their circumstances here are completely new so each character ends up with hours of individual exposition at minimum, and most chapters after Kiryu's don't really fold into the main plot until near the end.

- A lot of the central narrative is just flat out tangential or barely relevant, e.g. a troubled hunting village, idol competitions, baseball drama, etc. It's like half the staff didn't actually want to make another Yakuza game.

- Part 2 is miserably linear and three of the four chapters take place outside of any city, in scenarios where you walk around and talk to people to advance the plot, with a few scripted fights. Someone actually looked at the prison chapter in 4, said "yes, we need more of this", and put two chapters of barely interactive cutscenes and dialog here in 5 as well. The third chapter of Part 2 is basically plot setup for a minigame and has no relation to the plot or even the basic themes of the series. By the time you end up in a city and are free to move around on your own, it's underdeveloped like the other two new ones, with invisible walls everywhere. Somehow Saejima can shoot up a noodle shop, head his own organized crime family, and beat crowds of people half to death every 15 feet when he goes outside but jaywalking is beyond the pale.

- I don't like Shinada. His nasal voice is annoying, his fighting style sucks, and his whole dumb baseball story (minus the scant parts that relate to the yakuza) is really boring.

- The new cities are underwhelming. Play spots and other points of interest are sparse compared to Sotenbori and Kamurocho. In contrast to 4 where they fleshed out Kamurocho with multiple levels and collectables the cities in 5 all seem barren and undeveloped with nothing to explore. Just move from cutscene to cutscene and run through the substory checklist. Subjectively, I also just think they're dull to look at.

- The new minigames seem like obviously bad ideas, mainly in the sense that they all seem to revolve around established genres that usually get their own games with more thorough treatment (racing, hunting, rhythm). The racing and hunting minigames are on the level of mid-90s shareware and unsurprisingly not very great. I don't fault the devs for this outside of how they could have chosen something more appropriate. The rhythm parts in Haruka's section were sort of enjoyable and it's nice running around the city and dancing with people but the difficulty even on Hard is pitiful. I'm guessing since the rhythm sections are unavoidable, RGG Studio decided to tone down the challenge for everyone who isn't into this kind of thing and who expected a beat-em-up game like usual. That's understandable but if they couldn't go all the way with it, it probably wasn't a great idea to start with.

- The usual minigames are barely accessible for most of the game due to them being absent from cities or plot-restricted, sometimes for reasons that make sense (Haruka doesn't gamble), sometimes for reasons that don't (Kiryu can play exactly 2 (two) games of shogi in Kyuushuu before his opponent randomly packs up and leaves). Making things even worse is that the game has a random luck mechanic where you'll get cellphone messages periodically announcing whether you feel lucky/unlucky; this is basically the game announcing to you that the PRNG is now tilted for or against you in games of chance. As an example, I suck at mahjongg, yet on the first hand of my second game I scored suukantsu, the most improbable yakuman (outside of tenhou and chihou). After I picked my jaw up off the floor I realized the game had probably cheated for me and playing an honest game of mahjongg isn't an option in this installment (putting aside the fact that mahjongg isn't available for 2/3rds of the game anyhow).

- They went overboard with the heat attacks. I have no idea how many times I rolled my eyes after mistakenly pressing Y with a full heat gauge during a fight with random thugs and got stuck watching a 15 second movie of Akiyama kneeing some guy in the face. It gets old fast.

- Even though this has one of the best final chapters in the series, the plot twists and overall writing get pretty stupid toward the end.

I do not recommend this game except for die-hard fans of the series, and they shouldn't play the game without a walkthrough.  Most of the same problems with Yakuza 4 are in this game, so read that review for those things.  I played all the way through it on Normal difficulty.

However, they introduced new problems with this game, mostly linked to switching characters.  First, DO NOT get any of the locker keys with Haruka.  During the playthrough, you can't move things from her item box to other character AT ALL.  For instance, the Chunk of Ash needed to make a specific weapon - if you get it with Haruka, kiss it goodbye, because you can't get it any other way.

Second, the minigames cheat like hell this time, worse that Yakuza 4.  Sometimes your phone will tell you you have bad luck - believe it.  Sometimes it tells you you'll have good luck - DO NOT BELIEVE IT.  I like playing the Koi Koi card game, and on a "good luck" day, I got my ass handed to me and had to reload (and I play well enough to be able to score 9 platinum plates in a row, over 13000 points worth).  If you're going for 100% completion, you'll need over 20 million yen, because several of the weapons you need to craft are 800k - 1000k in price.  You'll need to gamble.  Save before gambling.

Fishing is basically impossible without a FAQ.  Getting the Maguro and Squid (not bait) for the weapons required a Google search.  Trying to do it on your own is not guaranteed, because you can get several types of fish and junk items with the same bait in the same range depending on day or night - bait costs add up, and selling fish doesn't make enough to buy more bait unless you catch a huge fish like a marlin or coelacanth.

The billiards and dart games get too hard at the advanced level, even with good dart parts.  It was better in Yakuza 0 where you got the best darts by buying them at the pawn shop, and when the game didn't mess with your aim in billiards - in short, it cheats a LOT.  And forget air hockey on the hard level - the only way to score is with heat shots, and the game loves to make you to chuck your puck in your own goal for no reason.

No pachinko or slots for the Remastered version is unfair, considering the PlayStation version still has it, and they have other gambling games like poker, blackjack, roulette, etc.

Winning at the gambling tables is more of a risk than the previous game, so keep those win items handy, and use them appropriately to win the most money.  The lack of save points make it a long run back to the casino, and you get in fights along the way, which is irritating considering the Kiwami 1 and 2 games allowed you to save anywhere.

But the worst thing about this game, by far and away, is the Coliseum.  You have to get to around 200 rank points just to break the top 10, and you only get 3 points a match (3 fights per tournament, 1 point per win).  It takes forever, but worse than that, once you get there, you get beaten to a pulp.  I'm not a young gamer - I'm good at this game, but even I have endurance limits.  When you break the top 10, the #1 guy cheats ALL THE TIME.  How?  Mohammed Ali style - when you start beating on him and gaining heat, he grabs you, and half your heat disappears before your pounding the A button will make him let go.  He does this EVERY time you gain heat.  My only match with him went around 10 - 15 minutes on him alone, not even counting the first two hard fights.  I DAMAGED my wrist and arm because I was constantly pounding the A keep to stop him from throwing me.  That's never happened to me before, ever.  My arm was so hot I couldn't keep it up.  He finally destroyed me, and that's the last time I'll ever play the Coliseum in Yakuza 5 again - probably the last time I'll ever play the game, period.  I love the story and the general mechanics, but they made it far too hard on Normal difficulty.  It was impossible for me to win, with an inventory full of Stamiman Sparks (full heal, full heat).  That should never have happened, especially with Saejima.  Oh, and you can't get any of the missable items at the Coliseum (nor levels to get Spirit Orbs), so it's not really worth it except for 100% completion.

But it did, and it happened again with the 2-on-1 fight in the Dojo with the baseball guy - they literally would not let me get a single hit in.  Without Kiryu's reversals and counterattacks, I just got beat to hell.  Saejima was the easiest to win with, and Kiryu was easy enough, but with the baseball guy it was impossible.  I gave up on Akiyama because of what happened with the baseball guy.

The Amon fight was even worst than the Coliseum.  I got through the first three all right, but with Kiryu, I got wiped.  Not only did it grab me all the time, draining all my heat, but I couldn't grab him back, EVER.  That's cheating.  Worse, when I switched to my no-break katana, I could not hit him without heat actions.  I managed to get the guy down to green, and it uncorked everything it had, blocking everything I did, unable to grab, it hit me with unblockables to the legs, and finished doing two of the main character's super moves BACK TO BACK.  I didn't stand a chance at that point.  Remember, this is supposed to be NORMAL mode.

No, you don't have to fight those battles.  I finished the game because I'd had enough of the AI cheating - the final story fight was easier by far, and I didn't even use any items to win it.  That's what made me angry.  The game shouldn't be this hard at Normal level, and it's not fun.  The inability to transfer items is not fun.  The game cheating at the minigames is not fun.  Yakuza 0, K1, K2 were fun, they didn't cheat so much.  Once you got all the skills, you were expected to maul everything in Normal mode.  Not in this game.

One last thing:  If you have no rhythm, and you hate games like Dance Dance Revolution and Guitar Hero, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.  Haruka's story is all about getting into dance battles, and the interface sucks.  Not only are button presses needed to be done in time with the music, you have to use the D-pad to chose which line you need to press the buttons on (there's 4 of them).  It's actually far worse than the usual too-fast karaoke minigame.  I don't do well with DDR-type games, but I barely made it through.  There is an Amon dance battle near the end - I tried it, it was the hard version of Haruka's initial song (twice as many buttons to mash), and after three unsuccessful tries, I gave up.  It's too hard for me, just like the karaoke stuff.  I never get 100% because of this stuff, and I hate that it's so hard, especially since you MUST succeed at these to advance the storyline.  I only managed it because the story mission difficulty remains at medium throughout.  It's quite generous considering how many presses I missed.  Too bad the Amon fight couldn't have been like that.  Poor QA in not getting things level for Normal mode.

So, don't play this unless you're a fan of the story and you're willing to skip 100% completion.  Play at your own risk.  It took two days for my arm to recover, and that was only playing games with my other hand (I'm lucky I use my mouse left-handed).  Stay away from the Coliseum, it's broken.  Save before doing the Coliseum, Amon or the Dojo fights, or you may burn all your items and still lose.  Same with the gambling.  If it's going to cheat, you might as well cheat by saving early and often.  If you have rhythm problems, take breaks between dance battles.  Save before every one.  Good luck, you'll need it if you play this game.

Steam's rating system is busted and I'm a fan of this series, but I still can't recommend this behemoth of a game, that is the literal definition of quantity over quality. Obviously if you're playing through these titles in order you may still wish to subject yourself to this fifth entry. If you are a completionist, then I pray Kami-sama have mercy on your soul.
Yakuza5 has, by far, the worst story among all the entries I've played so far, which includes all of them, and this means that I have a fairly high tolerance for the shenanigans Yakuza usually pulls and I'm ready to suspend by disbelief. I know that ultimately it's about naked guys smashing each other's faces in on a rooftop. But still somehow the other entries managed a far better way to tell their contrived plotlines (I don't include Zero here, which is the only one that is truly amazing). At one point the characters literally state out loud: 'let's fight until something happens' They fight. Then something happens which is not satisfying at all. Plot 'twist' after twist follows around, with everyone betraying everyone, but nobody actually having any sort of damn plan. Fights happen and that's mostly it.
Gameplay-wise I have to say that, yes, it's better than 4 and the combat is mostly enjoyable. If you don't count the many street thugs that force you into inescapable fights when you're just trying to get someplace. Each character has their own sidestories which range from fairly enjoyable to tedious. I appreciated some of them, including the taxi missions and even Saejima's hunting. Haruka's singing was... there, I guess. I didn't hate it but it went on for too long. Same with Shinada's story. He's not unlikable but his presence doesn't justify the hours it takes to get through his story.
Aside from all this mess there is your standard Yakuza stuff, with endlessly impossible minigames, training masters and lots of other activities you'll be too burned out to engage with.
Now all of this would be forgivable if it actually mattered. Unfortunately these last 3 entries (3,4,5) feel mostly like spin-offs, because they waste so much time in superflous dialogue and fail to make the connections that matter, focusing instead on characters that simply don't matter. For example, Haruka and Akyiama know each other here, despite me remembering too well that they never met in the previous game. Instead of wasting my time with useless thug banter or dine-and-dash substories, you could've spent some time establishing their relationship.
I'm complaining about this because these characters obviously have lots of potential and you get to spend A LOT of time with them, so you kinda just want more than this nonsense.
Still, I'm happy I got through all of these entries in my long journey across the Yakuza series. But Steam is asking me to recommend it and I just can't. But make your own decision. In the grand scheme of things, looking back on my entire journey with Yakuza, I'm happy I played them all, the worst and the best. But whether that is your goal or you have the patience for that, only you know.

in Yakuza 5, each characters takes a minimum of 10 hours. Without side quests, this game takes you 50 hours for the story . It is very hard to follow as there is a constant flow of newly introduced side characters for each protagonist. Furthermore, being required to start from scratch with each one after 10 hours of gameplay feels unrewarding and becomes tedious quickly.
Two protagonists have very lackluster stories, as one character has roughly the same story as in Yakuza 4, while the other is never mentioned again after this game and has a story that barely has anything to do with the main plot. The story itself is fairly uneventful; you can skip this game and proceed to Yakuza 6 without losing out on too many details.

The fighting is fun; Yakuza 5 offers four characters with wholly different fighting styles, although all of them need levelling.

Yakuza 5 tries few new things which it excels at, but due to the extremely long story with too many involved characters, along a horrible pacing and bad levelling the game turns into a convoluted mess that you wish would go by quicker.

There is no need to play this game unless you want to know everything about the franchise or the characters that appear in it.

"Slop 5 Remastered" is a 2019 remaster of an old 2012 Open world Beat Em' Up PS3 game called "Slop 5," which also came out on PC and Xbox in late 2021.

[b]Slop 5[/b] follows 5 different characters you can play as: Suzuki, Saejima, Haruka, Akiyama, and Shinada (Kiryu is staying out of this one this time /j) as you experience their daily lives until an incident happens that brings them all at the crossroads in Kamurocho once more to fight off some evil Yakuza with a Vendetta on them.

[b]The combat[/b] of Slop 5 Remastered remained relatively the same as the older Yakuza games, and the game now features 5 different cities, some of which are genuinely the best looking in the entire series. But sadly, the game doesn't let you explore them due to them being tied to the story, so it's just a whole-ass wasted potential. Kamurocho especially remained empty on side missions, so other than the finale, there's literally nothing to do on this copy-pasted map. But generally, when this game is trying to be Yakuza and not something else, it works really well.

Now when we get down to the story, it starts off relatively good. There's this sense of suspense and mystery behind the disappearance of the Tojo clan chairman, which I really liked and wanted to see what's gonna be next until the game showed me a giant middle finger and diverted my attention to some taxi driver submissions, most of which consist of talking to passengers or driving while obeying the traffic rules, which was generally boring. I already wanted to drop the game in the first 5 hours, but the wish of knowing what the hell happened to Daigo kept me going.

[b]Part 2 and 3 should've been cut or reduced to a cutscene or a series of flashbacks.[/b]
When you thought the game diverting your attention to the mundane taxi missions, which don't even matter on the grand scheme of things, was already bad enough, the game shows you an even bigger middle finger in Part 2, in which Saejima escapes from prison AGAIN. This would've been fine on its own since we get to know the new cast of characters and his new sworn brother, but what makes my blood boil is what happens after that. As you're already starving to see the story, some epic plot twist, or anything regarding Kiryu’s part, the game diverts your attention AGAIN and becomes a frickin HUNTING SIMULATOR??? WHAT WERE THEY THINKING? Why in the god's name would I wanna hunt a bear in a game about crime dramas and hand on hand combat? And the worst thing is the gunplay in this hunting simulator is not even good; it's shallow, doesn't have an impact, and takes absolutely 0 skill. So why the hell would they add this other than to add more filler to an already bloated game is beyond me.

And what is worse is [b]Part 3.[/b] As you're spiraling down your sanity of wanting to see a great story, the game shows you a middle finger a size of a Millennium tower instead cause F*ck you! You're playing as HARUKA now! My first genuine reaction was WTF, how would she battle enemies? Oh wait what? Dance battle? Oh, that makes sense cause she's an idol now! The entire part which took me around 7 hours to beat consists of playing this terrible project diva knockoff minigame that only has 3 songs that you're gonna have to play at least a dozen times. And memorizing all the patterns to each song makes this whole chapter stale as a crusty Stalin's foot as they force you to play the same songs on repeat, which your mind can't even take it anymore. If only it had more compositions or different patterns every time, it would've been tolerable a bit. Overall this Part, despite being important to the story unlike 2, which could be described in 1 sentence, literally bored me out of my mind, and I don't understand why it would ever be included in a game about Yakuza families.

[b]Part 4 is a breath of fresh air…[/b]As it introduces a new character into the mix - Tatsuo Shinada, a former baseball player that got banned from the game for suspicion of stealing enemy's signals. And a return to the classic beat 'em up Yakuza formula. This chapter was very enjoyable as it has very charismatic characters, engaging substories, a new city, and much-needed humor. Shinada, despite being piss broke, is very determined in his goal, confronting his demons and finding out the truth about his expulsion. If only every other Part of Slop 5 was like this one this would've been the greatest game in the series in my eyes.

Every character in Slop 5 has a unique move set which you can learn and master throughout their respected Parts, I'd even say you'd get way too much time to master them cause even traversing around towns is a pain in the ass since you can't take 2 steps without a random encounter, and it gets really annoying. Learning the combat thoroughly doesn't really make much sense either unless you're planning on doing a legendary difficulty playthrough in which case yeah, you're gonna need that knowledge. Otherwise, most bosses and encounters can be cheesed by using the same move the enemy is weak against, therefore rendering the entire move system useless.

[b]The finale[/b] surely has one of the most ambitious final bosses in the series if only there was a way to not cheese him by using the same move 300 times. Another thing that disappointed me that all the skills and stats you grinded throughout the game simply don’t matter in the final encounters, especially for Haruka since you don’t even get to perform the songs as her what a shame and what a butt hurt that caused me when I realized I spent hours doing godawful side missions and maxing out the stats mattered to nothing. And the cliffhanger ending didn’t help my scorched butt either as it was reaching the critical temperatures of 100 billion degrees Celsius after realizing that I spent 50 hours on an empty shell of a game that looks huge at first but at its core, it’s a glorified artificially extended with filler and copy-pasted missions slop.

[b]The PC port performance[/b] was pleasant overall other than a minor glitch that would occasionally randomize audio in the cutscenes.

Overall, [b]Slop 5 is a type of game that tries to be everything at once but fails to innovate on anything[/b], therefore, everything more or less feels like a huge filler in this game. Like George R.R Martin once said in Family Guy, “You just took a lot of pills, mashed a bunch of sci-fi and cliché together, and crapped out a 2000-page turd.” Since the game constantly revolves around dreams and family, I can only dream of a better game after beating Slop 5. This will remain as my most unfavorite game and a resemblance of 50+ hours of my life that I'm never getting back.
